utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. We can now proceed to hear the closing arguments on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At the beginning I just want to say that me and my colleague Ivetic divided our work, so at the beginning I will do my part and after that, Mr. Ivetic will probably do the major part of our closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And because of the speed, I'll speak in Serbian and because of the speed Mr. Ivetic will speak in English. [Interpretation] So once again, good day, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Lukic will attempt to put forward in a brief outline its case; and to begin with, I would like to refer to what my colleagues have already spoken about, the plan, the alleged plan, to expel Albanians. I think that my colleagues from the other Defence teams have provided numerous arguments. I will deal with a small segment of this issue, and what I wish to add is the following. It is not contested that before all of these events Serbia was a signatory of the Dayton Accords, which referred to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those accords were signed in 1995 when hostilities ceased in this former Yugoslav republic. Annex 7 of those accords refers to the return of refugees and displaced persons. Can one imagine that someone who had direct experience with war, the departure and return of refugees in his immediate neighbourhood could imagine that the same rules would not apply to him? Can anyone in their right mind think that Slobodan Milosevic did not know that refugees, should there be any refugees, would not return to their homes once hostilities ceased? To me, it doesn't seem like common sense. The participants in this agreement were inter alia Slobodan Milosevic and Wesley Clark, so there was nothing unknown on that terrain. Everything had already been a subject of long-term negotiations, agreements, treaties, and the implementation of all this. Up to the outbreak of war in Serbia in 1999, most of the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina who wanted to had returned to their homes. International organizations were helping to rebuild their homes and to enable sustainable return. One should know that the Dayton Accords of 1999 were a daily topic in the Serbian media, as they were a daily topic in the media of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and it was also something that those who had fled to Serbia from Bosnia spoke about every day and they intended to return to Bosnia. So these accords were discussed in Serbia daily. The return of refugees from Serbia to Bosnia was a Serbian problem, so this was what was happening in 1998 and 1999 on a daily basis in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do we have any evidence of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Line 7, would return, not would not return.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- it's commonly known fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly not a commonly known fact to me, but if there is evidence it would be helpful if you could point to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'll try to do it when Mr. Ivetic continues his part, I'll try to find it. Thank you. [Interpretation] According to the Prosecutor, someone had the bright idea of expelling Albanians but first they said, Let's provoke NATO to bomb us. That is not a case which our Defence finds at all credible. I will paraphrase now and deal with what was achieved by the alleged plan to expel Albanians according to the Prosecutor. According to the Prosecutor, the expulsion was already completed for the most part in mid-April 1999, a third of the Albanians had been expelled and now there were only five times more Albanians than there were Serbs, while before there were eight times more. Does this sound credible? How has this changed the ethnic balance in favour of Serbs and what sort of balance has been achieved. Witness Haxhibeqiri said, referring to Djakovica, that there were two to three per cent Serbs in Djakovica, so how many Albanians would have to be expelled from Djakovica in order to establish an ethnic balance. The Prosecutor has failed to show this and he has failed to show that this was done. The next point I wish the Chamber to pay attention to is the following. Wouldn't it be logical for Serbs to expel Albanians from those parts of Kosovo where there was no KLA, from those parts where they were allegedly not protected? Why would the Serbs be expelling Albanians from areas where there was the highest concentration of KLA? What sort of logic is that? Who in their right minds would push their people to get killed when they could do this, whatever they wanted to do, elsewhere with no problems at all? Now I would like to move on to the main topic of our Defence case, and that is the MUP staff and Exhibit P1505, which is a decision on the establishment of the staff dated the 16th of June, 1998. By means of this document, the Prosecutor wishes to show who were members of the staff and what the tasks of the staff were. Our Defence says the following. This document never came to life, either as regards personnel or as regards functioning. Numerous witnesses have testified about these circumstances and written evidence has also been presented which clearly shows that this decision never came to life. We dealt with this in paragraph 690 to 785 of our final brief, and the OTP dealt with it in paragraphs 208 to 211 of their final brief. In the course of this trial we have heard the testimony of Mijatovic, Adamovic, we have seen documents on the appointment and the termination of duties of some persons, and those are 6D1044 to 6D1052. We will prove, and I think we have proved - but we will show this today - that the members of the staff from the first page of the decision did not include David Gajic; Radoslav Djinovic; Milorad Lukovic, Legija; and Zivko Trajkovic. You can see that from the testimony of Miroslav Mijatovic. We saw that while the staff existed there were personnel changes in the composition of the staff more than once. No decision was issued about that in terms of establishing the staff. So this is a legally imperfect situation but it was what it was. We saw that at the outset. After the issuing of this decision, Miroslav Mijatovic arrived. In the summer of 1998 Dusko Adamovic arrived, after the decision had already been issued, and Desimir Slovic also arrived. The three of them were members of the staff according to what Miroslav Mijatovic, Dusko Adamovic, and Radovan Vucurevic said. We see this from the personnel decisions. For example, Radoslav Djinovic on the 19th of June, 1998, stopped being deployed in Kosovo. We saw that Dusko Adamovic left Kosovo because he was wounded when the staff was bombed, although this is not mentioned in this decision, he is not mentioned, and he left according to the decision of the 1st of April, but as Vucurevic said, they already left on the 20th of March, the same day when they were wounded. On the 29th of March, Desimir Slovic also left Kosovo, and he again is not mentioned in this decision, and he was a member of the staff and was wounded when the staff was bombed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Line 17, the 29th of March, not the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 15th of February before this bombing, Novica Zdravkovic left. So as of the 15th of February, he was no longer a member of the staff and he was replaced by Tomislav Blagojevic. After they left, that is, Adamovic, Slovic, and Vucurevic, on the 29th of March Milenko Arsenijevic took their place as did Petar Bogdanovic and Voja Gucic. In Mijatovic's testimony and in our final brief the documents speaking to this are enumerated. We are convinced that we have managed to prove that the decision of the 16th of June, 1998, to establish the MUP staff never came to life as regards unifying the state security and public security departments within the staff. And that we have proved that David Gajic and Milorad Lukovic, Legija, were not members of the staff; and this was confirmed by all the members of the staff who testified here. This is also evident from documents. When members of the staff are listed in documents, especially members of the state security, for example, P1099 and P2085. We proved that Zivko Trajkovic, the commander of the SAJ, was not a member of the staff either. All the members of the staff confirmed this, witness Joksic on transcript page 22026, and this was confirmed by Radovan Vucurevic on page 23056 of the transcript. Milos Vojnovic on page 24148. We also see this from the statement of Dusko Adamovic in 6D1613, paragraph 7; then Bozidar Filic on page 23949 and 23965 of the transcript. The next point that has to do with the staff personnel are the members of the SUP -- the chiefs of SUP and the chiefs of the state security department. We are convinced that we have managed to prove in the course of these proceedings that the chiefs of the SUPs and the chiefs of the state security departments in Kosovo and Metohija were not members of the staff, although that's what it says in the decision on establishing the staff. According to this decision, the members of the extended staff would include those persons but that they were not members of the staff was also confirmed by Cvetic Ljubinko on transcript page 8146, and this can be seen from Exhibits P1099 and P2805. It's clear then that the decision on establishing the staff never came to life as regards personnel. Mr. Lukic's Defence has dealt with this in its final brief in paragraphs 731 to 755. In point 2 in the same decision, the tasks of the staff are listed and when the OTP describes the tasks of the staff it relies on this decision exclusively without analysing the other evidence adduced in the course of these proceedings. We dealt with this in paragraph 756 to 766 of our final brief, our closing brief. During the proceedings here, we have shown that this situation, that is, that the staff never began to function in the way envisaged by the decision on the forming of the staff for the reason that terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija had escalated to such an extent that a five-stage plan for fighting against terrorism had been adopted at the state level. And the authority to plan activities in relation to anti-terrorist action was removed from the MUP and given to the Army of Yugoslavia. After the global five-stage plan for the fight against terrorism was adopted, which was drawn up by the Pristina Corps according to Djakovic, who testified here, the planning of individual -- joint actions was carried out by the Pristina Corps according to Witness Djakovic, and the excerpts on the maps were delivered to the MUP staff or directly to the PJP detachments. And on the basis of this, the PJP detachments went into action. The MUP staff neither amended or modified these plans in any way. It simply forwarded them to the PJP units, as testified by Witness Dusko Adamovic. We have shown and proved that not a single plan for the carrying out of joint actions of the police and the army was drawn up in the staff. To say the least, the OTP and the Defence teams of the military generals, in spite of all their attempts, have not succeeded in proving such a case. No one has ever seen such a document ever because there is no such document in existence. In the course of these proceedings, attempts were made to say that 6D716 was drawn up in the MUP staff because it says "MUP command" on it. But Mile Djakovic confirmed that he compiled this document and that it is not, in fact, an order, simply a document showing something. This role of the staff as regards planning, the planning of anti-terrorist actions, that is, seemed incredible at the beginning of our Defence case and His Honour Judge Bonomy asked whether this meant that the staff was simply a letter box. The claims made by Mijatovic who told the Chamber that they would get more information about this from Adamovic, and this was confirmed by Dusko Adamovic himself. But we still think that our witnesses were not given credence at that point. The reason for this is that many testimonies from military witnesses about this were heard and they all explained what it was that Mile Djakovic was doing and they all claimed that it was the MUP that made the orders and the excerpts on the maps, those who testified to this. But no one except Stefanovic finally confirmed that it was possible that some excerpts on the maps were sent to the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that there is a sudden echo in the room. Could that be seen to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Djakovic confirmed that all the excerpts on the map were made by the Pristina Corps and sent to the MUP staff. He was shown maps for detachment level and PJP company level, both for 1998 and for 1999, and he confirmed that they were all compiled by the Pristina Corps staff in which he himself worked, or rather, people who worked for him. The excerpts on the maps were produced for the SAJ and JSO, and this can be seen from the following exhibits in this case: 4D495, 6D619, 6D1620, 6D1621; and for SAJ: 5D1329. Zivaljevic explained when testifying before this Trial Chamber that the commanders of the detachments could not plan actions if nothing -- for no other reason than for technical reasons. Not only did they not have the necessary knowledge, for example, Zivaljevic had not attended military academy at all, but the MUP detachments had no staffs. So quite simply there wasn't anybody who could do that, and this is to be found on the transcript page 24820/12 to 19. Witness Ilic in response to a question from Mr. Bakrac explained that nobody in the police force had the necessary knowledge to plan any kind of action which went beyond the level of a company and this is to be found on transcript page 24359/21 to T24360/4. Furthermore, we showed that neither the staff nor Sreten Lukic commanded PJP units on the ground nor did they lead any anti-terrorist actions. The PJP had a separate structure from the staff and all commanders of the PJP from top to bottom, including the commander of the PJP himself, throughout the actions were in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, both in 1998 and in 1999. And there were a large number of documents and testimonies to bear that out, and this is particularly dealt with in paragraphs 676 to 773 of our brief. When the PJP commander on the ground -- was on the ground, then I assume it is clear that there can be no parallel command. Who would meddle in any of this from outside? Communication means necessary for commanding units were not accessible to the staff and we heard testimony about this by Defence Witness Deretic and this particularly refers to 1999 when the MUP staff had no means of communication whatsoever in Kosovo and Metohija except for a courier service. It was not possible to command units of the courier service. They had to have communication devices in order to maintain communications, so even if they had wanted to - and they certainly did not - and even if they were authorised - and they certainly were not - the members of the staff would not have been able to command the combat units of the MUP. We provided to the Court and the Prosecution all the daily reviews of the events compiled by the MUP staff, all of them, from July 1998 right up until the 20th of June, 1999. I apologise, I meant to say the 10th of June, 1999. They are not all exhibits in this case but they can be easily checked out because the Prosecution has them and the Trial Chamber has them, and we maintain, the Defence of Mr. Lukic maintains that not in a single one of them is there a report from the PJP on combat actions, not in a single one of them. Of course all this holds true for the daily reviews that are part of the documents in this case. A decision to set up the staff and headquarters did not come into effect when it came to the staff guiding and coordinating the work of MUP units in KiM, SUPs, MUPs, border police stations all come under those work organization units. During proceedings we showed the way in which planning worked, we showed in which the way leadership worked, and in which way reporting worked within MUP, and by the same token within the SUP in Kosovo and Metohija it is clear that the staff is not present in any segment of planning and leadership for the work of SUP and smaller organizational units. The only field where the staff does appear is the field of reporting. You will not find the staff anywhere else outside the reporting field, and we see that the staff was informed from the ministry downwards, so from top to bottom, and in parallel fashion when the SUP were informed, and from bottom to the top by the SUPs from Kosovo and Metohija in parallel fashion and up to the head seat of the ministry. And this is evidenced in P1044. And linked to that, the Prosecution in its final brief provided us with a schematic of MUP, a diagram produced by Philip Coo, before any evidence was produced. This diagram has nothing to do with reality and does not reflect the actual situation and therefore cannot be used for any purposes or in any sense. The Prosecution in claiming that the staff, and thereby Sreten Lukic was in a position of superiority to the police in Kosovo and Metohija, claimed that the staff was in fact the ministry in small. The staff should have been paralleled with the provincial secretariat for the interior, and we heard that that secretariat had a thousand employees, whereas the staff just had ten members or even less. The number of policemen, while the provisional secretariat was in existence, was almost the same as the number of policemen that existed in 1999 and 1998; and we heard testimony about this from Bozidar Filic. Therefore, with the establishment of the staff the chains of planning were not interrupted of leadership and reporting within the frameworks of MUP. The staff and not Sreten Lukic either had effective control over the police in Kosovo and Metohija in the critical period. I should like to stress that the -- neither the staff nor Sreten Lukic were able to initiate disciplinary measures and proceedings against members of the MUP, they had no role in any of that and could not have had and could not have taken part in any of that, neither the staff nor Sreten Lukic, either in criminal proceedings or in misdemeanour proceedings against policemen in Kosovo and Metohija. There were many, many documents to bear this out, 6D464, 6D1339, 6D1340, 6D1343, 6D1344, 6D1345, 6D1346, and so on and so forth. There are many documents testifying to this that speak about disciplinary measures and criminal proceedings. This general area is regulated in detail by provisions, so we cannot accept the claims of the Prosecution that Sreten Lukic was a general and therefore, by the same token, he must have wielded influence. There is nothing like that in the police force. It's a well-ordered system. It is a system ordered by provisions, and each person's power and authority are precisely determined. You can't say that somebody certainly has influence or certainly does not have influence. Even a Prosecution witness by the name of Cvetic confirmed that the MUP staff had nothing whatsoever to do with these procedures and therefore need not have even been informed about any of this, and this is to be found on transcript page 8152. Only with lacking this segment in the hands of the staff and Sreten Lukic, we clearly see that there was no effective control by the staff. Had they had everything else in their hands, if they were not able to initiate proceedings to take disciplinary measures, then they could not have had effective control. Furthermore, neither the MUP staff nor Sreten Lukic could have appointed anyone or relieved anyone of their duties, that is to say policemen in Kosovo and Metohija, they were not able to replace a single policeman. And we deal with this in our brief paragraph 675 to 685. And there's another essential point. The MUP staff is not an organizational unit of the MUP either, it does not have the authorisation or rights of an ordinary organizational unit. A part of SUP, the territorial part of SUP, is an organizational unit, the staff is not. During these proceedings we have seen a number of minutes from meetings held in the MUP staff and that's what it said, they weren't staff meetings. The only minutes from a staff meeting is the minutes that are denoted as P3120, dated the 23rd of July, 1998, and these minutes from the meetings held in the MUP staff were held once a month, as the Prosecutor noted himself. Now, can -- could one command an action by holding meetings just once a month? Would that be feasible? Is that the way in which actions were commanded? And that's what we find in the Prosecution's final brief in paragraph 214. All the meetings in 1999 during the war were attended by Obrad Stevanovic. He was in Kosovo and Metohija and had all the authority from the minister as being his assistant, and it was as if the minister had attended those meetings. Now, we brought a police -- we brought an expert for police matters. The Prosecution failed to do that. They couldn't find anybody to claim what they were saying, not even Babovic they couldn't even bring Babovic in, and they challenged the credibility of our expert and they say that he didn't deal with the police in Kosovo in his work. Nobody dealt with the police in Kosovo at that time because nothing like that existed at that time. What did exist was the police of the Republic of Serbia. The Republic of Kosovo did not exist and by the same token the police of Kosovo did not exist in 1998 and 1999. It simply did not exist and nobody dealt with those matters because the body did not exist. I'd now like to discuss the importance of Sreten Lukic's role. Many people testified here about that. Now, if some people from outside were to observe Sreten Lukic -- well, it would depend how they viewed him, in what field, in what area. If they looked at him as somebody who provided information, then he appeared important because that was his job. It was his job to know about the security situation in Kosovo. In 1998 he sent feedback information to the SUPs, he sent back information, the information he had gathered, to the SUPs in Kosovo and the headquarters in Belgrade. Once the war broke out, that was no longer possible so the information was just sent to MUP headquarters in Belgrade. However, if observers met him in conditions where decisions were called for, then they would have gained the impression that his function and post carried no weight at all. For example, Aleksandar Vasiljevic, a Prosecution witness, has told you here that he was not the number one man but the number ten man. He said this referring to his role in the middle of the war, and during that time the OTP claims that Lukic was the senior officer of MUP in Kosovo and Metohija. And Vasiljevic was testifying about the 1st of June, 1999. Later on the Prosecution changed this and said that Lukic was the highest appointed official in Kosovo and Metohija. Obrad Stevanovic, when he arrives in Kosovo and Metohija or any other functionary from the headquarters or Dragan Ilic, general, the head of the criminal -- the crime police, he was the be-all and end-all. They were the ones who decided what was going to be done. They didn't ask Sreten Lukic, they didn't report to him. They would inform him if they wanted to do so on a need-to-know basis; if not, they wouldn't. General Ojdanic as the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command describes him as an adjutant in the middle of the war on the 11th of April, 1999, and this is to be found in Exhibit 3D1125 on page 75. Sakic claims that Protic told him that Lukic didn't give him an apartment when he was chief of the public security department and that he was the fifth wheel again and second violin and this is to be found on transcript page 22156. After the war Sreten Lukic was appointed to a post where a colonel -- the rank of colonel would have been sufficient, whereas he had the rank of lieutenant-general. Naumann doesn't remember Lukic having been present at meetings at all and this is to be found in the transcript on page 8378. Judge Bonomy, you asked him: "Was Mr. Lukic present at any of these meetings?" And he says: "I don't remember." The agreement and the annex was signed by Djordjevic and Byrnes, and it is something that exclusively refers to Kosovo and Metohija. This annex relates specifically to KiM. We will see that at meetings Gajic was separately informed from Lukic and he was subordinate to him. It would be sufficient if Lukic were to report for both of them, surely. Abrahams doesn't write to Lukic, doesn't write letters to Lukic in 1998. Dimitrijevic doesn't claim that for Kosovo and Metohija Lukic was the main person. So if we look at the segment of decision-making and leadership, then there's no staff there and there's certainly no Lukic there either. And this brings us to why the new government decided to as the take is to include Sreten Lukic in the security department and Mr. Zivkovic testified to that, the former premier, and he explained the type of information they required both from domestic and foreign intelligence agents and agencies. The OTP attempts to draw an inference from 1998 to 1999. They say that what happened in 1998 certainly happened in 1999 also, and we say this is not correct and that the evidence shows it is not correct. Some of the elements which certainly cannot relate to both time-periods are the following. As we know, on the 24th of March, 1999, the NATO air-strikes began. This was something that was not happening in 1998. A state of war was declared and this means that there was specific circumstances such as mobilisation which did not obtain before. Some laws and bylaws came into force which were not in force in peacetime. The numbers of the KLA increased from 18.000, it increased greatly and the KLA began forcible mobilisation. In 1999 the KLA was much better organized and Mr. Byrnes worked a lot on that. He worked on the organization of the KLA, they were better armed. And this was done for the most part during the stay of the KVM in Kosovo. The KLA took territory and was preparing for a spring offensive and for cooperation with NATO. And we heard in the course of these proceedings that they did cooperate, that they did provide NATO with information. In Rule 70 documents we saw the manner in which this was done, we saw how they sent information to the other side which was bombing Serbia regarding the precision and success of the air-strikes. In 1999 urban terrorism escalated. It should be observed that NATO was bombing columns of civilians returning to their houses, to their homes, in Korisa and Bistrazin. Not a single column leaving the country was bombed. Not a single bridge, road, or railway leading out of the country towards Macedonia or Albania from Kosovo and Metohija was bombed, not a single one. And now briefly about the engagement of the MUP in 1998 first. As the KLA committed the most brutal crimes in 1998, murders, abductions, and so on, the MUP of Serbia was obliged under the law to take measures to prevent these crimes. They were duty-bound to do so by the Law on Criminal Procedure, the Law on Ministries, the Law on the Interior on Internal Affairs, and many other pieces of legislation. There was no special decision needed for the engagement of the MUP, no special decision, least of all a decision by the president of the FRY, Slobodan Milosevic. The MUP was simply acting in accordance with the law, both as a whole and each individual member of the MUP did the same. They didn't need anyone's decision to do that. When terrorist activities outgrew the ability of the MUP to deal with that evil and to protect the citizens, the state leadership of the FRY decided to engage the Army of Yugoslavia, and this began in July 1998. Before that, the state leadership reached a decision that the plan should be made. The plan was drawn up by the army. When the plan was adopted, it began to be implemented through the planning of individual actions. And let us repeat that the MUP staff for KiM never drew up these plans, either in 1998 or in 1999, although this is listed as one of its tasks in the decision on its establishment dated the 16th of June, 1998. And now briefly about the credibility of witnesses. We have seen that the OTP objected to the credibility of Defence witnesses because they were participants in these events, and truly the Defence did attempt to bring in as many witnesses as possible who did participate in these events and have first-hand knowledge. Does this mean that only witnesses with second-hand knowledge are credible? That's what the OTP would seem to claim. The OTP was able to examine each of our witnesses. They were able to collect documents to impeach our witnesses. And as we have seen, it was far easier for the OTP to gain -- to obtain documents than it was for the Defence. For example, Cedomir Sakic's statement, which the Defence attempted to obtain for a year with no success. You know that we were engaged in litigation with either the FRY or Serbia and Montenegro. We had great problems with the MUP of Serbia; they wouldn't allow us access to documents. When we finally managed to gain access to documents, they punished the person who made it possible for us to access the documents acting on the minister's orders. The situation has improved recently, we have to admit. But this meant that we were short of time and that we were late in obtaining evidence we needed. Let me stress briefly that Adamovic is misquoted in paragraph 215 of the OTP final brief. He is not speaking about a meeting of the staff but about the meeting at which the five-stage plan was discussed with members of the army. This was not a meeting held in the MUP staff. It was quite a different meeting, but this is misinterpreted here and you can see this from Adamovic's testimony. Now we wish to refer Albanian witnesses. Very often one had the impression that witnesses who were Albanians and who were allegedly victims of crimes had been instructed on what to say. For example, what they say about the armbands they saw on the Serb forces, that is, the members of the MUP at the beginning of the air-strikes from the 24th of March until mid-April. It can be seen from the evidence that members of the MUP did not wear armbands before the 15th of April, 1999; however, Albanian witnesses described armbands which must have been shown to them from photographs of the police in 1998 and this is best illustrated by the fact that they often saw the police wearing white armbands. In 1999 the police did not wear white armbands at all. Before the 15th of April, 1999, they wore no armbands and throughout 1999 they never wore white armbands. Every witness who claims to have seen a policeman with a white armband is not telling the truth, he has been instructed to say that based on photographs taken in 1998. We have also seen that all the witnesses of Albanian ethnicity deny that the KLA was present in the villages. This is contrary to all the evidence, combat reports, the testimony of Zyrapi, and so on. We see that actions and combat were conducted only in villages where the KLA was present. Of course, the two-villages tactic was used as General Lazarevic explained to us, but no action was undertaken unless the KLA had first conducted an attack. We saw the testimony of Witness Gavranic for the territory of Gnjilane. The KLA was present there but they did not attack the police and the army and no anti-terrorist actions were conducted on his territory except for two in marginal areas in the direction of other municipalities because there was no need, no one had been attacked, although there was intelligence to show that the KLA was present there. However, the fact that they did not attack the police was sufficient for there not to be any anti-terrorist actions in the area. Of course the witnesses are afraid, very afraid. It wasn't that someone paid them not to tell the truth or asked them not to tell the truth. Most of them were probably afraid for their lives because we know what happened in other cases where Albanians were accused. We saw the situation described by Shaban Fazliu, the situation prevailing in Kosovo. The KLA is in control of Kosovo today and of course an Albanian testifying in open session here will not tell us what he knows. As regards credibility, I will comment briefly on Protic and Sakic. Protic arrived, and in the evaluation of this Defence team he lied shamelessly in certain parts of his testimony. The OTP says that what he claims is for the most part true. The Defence does not deny that he participated in transporting the bodies but that is not crucial for this case. What is crucial for this case is what contacts he had with Sreten Lukic. He was brought here to incriminate Sreten Lukic, not to tell us about the transport of the bodies. We heard about that from other witnesses, from people working on investigations, from people who exhumed the bodies. There's nothing being challenged there. What is being challenged is what contacts he had with Sreten Lukic. Does anyone in this courtroom know how many times Protic allegedly called Sreten Lukic or the voice which to him sounded like Sreten Lukic? Was it three times, two times, or only once? We don't know because it all depends on which of his statements we read. On page 11310 my learned friend Mr. Stamp put to Protic that he testified in Belgrade three times. He said, "You have had an opportunity to review the record of these three different occasions when you spoke about these events in 1999?" And Protic says: "Yes, after each of my testimonies I was given records of my testimony." And Mr. Stamp: "And was what you said in each one of these three occasions true to the best of your knowledge and belief?" And Protic said: "Yes, of course." And then the first disaster that Protic was engaged in took place. Stamp asked him about the voice which sounded like Sreten Lukic and now things become complicated. Protic says that Lukic addressed him by his first name Bozidar in all his statements, and yet here before this Tribunal he said three or four times that Sreten Lukic addressed him by his last name, Protic. We find this on page 11311, 11312, 11313 of the transcript. Judge Bonomy -- well, at the insistence of His Honour Judge Bonomy my learned friend Mr. Stamp asked him again and tried again to get him to say that Sreten Lukic addressed him by his first name, but he persisted in saying that Sreten addressed him by his last name. According to Protic, he went to the staff in order to call the staff; that's his testimony. According to him, on each of those three occasions he happened to be given a telephone which had a direct line with Belgrade. Among the large number of telephones where you had to dial the extension for Belgrade, three times by accident, without anyone to assist him, he happened to grab a telephone which had a direct connection. And witness Deretic explained how many such telephones there might have been in the staff during the war, one or two, and both in the same office. So if one were to analyse this evidence, Protic enters an office and uses a telephone which is in the same office where Sreten Lukic is answering the telephone. Then on page 11329 my learned friend Mr. Stamp tells him that he called Sreten Lukic three times, so each time he called Sreten Lukic. The first time he explains but he wasn't sure on cross-examination whether he was dialling a Belgrade number. The second time he explained again how he dialled the number, what sort of voice he heard, and so on. But in cross, again he's not sure what city he called. And then we come to the third occasion, we'll take this as our example to illustrate all this, he explains and says, This person told me to go to the parking lot behind Rilindija and there were trucks there. I would be met there by some men who would tell me which truck to take. There were four or five other trucks on the parking lot and I was to take only one. That's on transcript page 11327. On page 11328 my learned friend Mr. Stamp asked him: "On that occasion you took the bodies to the 13th May police centre in Batajnica. Why did you take the bodies there? "A. That's what I was told. "Q. By who? "A. The voice I had a telephone contact with." During cross-examination Protic admitted that he didn't call anyone the third time. So all these explanations are false, fabricated. He is not telling the truth. In his statements Protic said that the liaison person was a man waiting for him in a burgundy-coloured Golf, but he denied that before the Court and said he had never seen that man's face and that this man met him only once when he was going to Janjevo. The next thing Protic claims is that he had been Sreten Lukic's driver for six months, he was the personal driver of Sreten Lukic for six months, and he repeats that here too. He repeats that on page 11329. He says: "I was able to recognise his voice because I was his driver for six months." Later on on page 11330 he claims again that he was Lukic's driver. During the cross-examination on page 11377 he says that he wasn't Sreten's driver but Obrad Stevanovic's driver and that perhaps from time to time he might have driven Sreten Lukic somewhere, and he repeats that later on at 11378 and 11379. And he acknowledges that Sreten Lukic had his own driver who was another person and also confirms that he never drove Sreten Lukic after July 1990 and this is on page 11380. And he said that he'd never even talked to Sreten after the time he left Kosovo in 1990. So nine years went by since the time when he talked to Sreten Lukic for the last time and it was only several times before that. I should like to stress that Protic was a person who entered a flat illegally, a policeman looting a flat and moving into it, and he asked Sreten Lukic to legalise this illegal entry into that flat which the latter refused to do. Sreten Lukic refused to have any contact with him when he asked him for advice as to what to testify in reference to this indictment and the counts in it. So he's angry with Sreten for having sent him to the south of Serbia, he's angry with Sreten for having retired him. Well, had Sreten Lukic considered that he was guilty and that this man had something to hide, he surely would have wanted to satisfy him and meet his requirements rather than act contrary to what he demanded had he thought there was any danger and had he had anything to hide. There was discussion whether he told the truth in Belgrade. Judge Bonomy asked him. He said, Yes, I did tell the truth in Belgrade. Then he said, No, I didn't tell the truth in Belgrade, in fact, I'm telling the truth here and now. He changed his testimony in that respect. With regard to the credibility of Protic's testimony we heard testimony from a number of witnesses and we pin-pointed Aleksandar Kostic and Sakic, Kostic regularly cooperates with the Prosecution of this Tribunal, and Dragan Furdulovic, another witness. It is clear that all of them expressed doubt as to the credibility of the testimony of Bozidar Protic. Witness Sakic who took part in the events painted quite a different picture than the one painted by Protic, particularly with respect to the critical part, that is to say how Protic calls him and he says that it's not true that Protic used a stable telephone line but used a mobile telephone, that it was not true that he separated from him, that it was not true that they turned in to Pristina and went to the centre of Pristina and so on and so forth. We'd like to stress that had the Prosecution had Mr. Sakic's statement given to the investigating organs in Serbia, as we said the statement was not accessible to General Lukic's Defence or Sakic himself, and this is the way in which the MUP treated the Lukic Defence, an illustration of that. It is quite obvious that Sakic said the same thing in Belgrade that he told the Court here and he confirmed this when I asked him that, that is to be found on transcript page 22161, and I'd like to point out that the Prosecution did not include Sakic's statement in Belgrade because it's obvious that in fact he testified here in this court the same as he did in Belgrade many years before. Now, as far as the transportation of bodies is concerned, I don't think it was shown that the staff or that Sreten Lukic had anything to do with any of that. Of course we have to exclude Protic there. I think I have sufficient elements to prove to the Trial Chamber that they should not believe him and not trust him and not trust his credibility. As far as the transport of bodies is concerned, we heard testimony from Gvozden Gagic and saw the discussions held in the staff. We saw that General Ilic spent time in Kosovo and Metohija during that period, from the 23rd of May to the 1st of June, 1999, and (redacted)

utterances.text: Well, please continue then, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I want to remind you that these proceedings are to be viewed in a serious manner, not only because of the crimes that are alleged being serious but also because of the severity of the potential and unjust harm that could result to an innocent accused such as, we submit, Mr. Lukic, if the Prosecution case is to be believed. Given the severity of the foregoing, it is truly astounding to me the manner in which the Prosecution has prosecuted this case, without regard for detail, without regard for getting it right. They have recycled allegations and ignored the evidence that we have all heard in the interim two years of trial. Yet, this is apparently the best case the Prosecution cares to put forth after two years of trial. Your Honours, at the outset I wish to remind you that you have a dual responsibility for, just as you have a duty to provide justice to victims, you also have a duty and obligation to protect and uphold the rights of the accused including ensuring that the findings are based upon full and true facts, not mis-characterizations by the Prosecution, not guilt by association, and lastly you have a duty to uphold the right of freedom and acquittal for an innocent accused when the facts so dictate. This needs to be borne in mind for this is a case where countless Prosecution witnesses came and changed their story, dramatically changed their previous sworn testimony and statements upon appearing at this trial with this Prosecution. I call upon you to recall your own words, Judge Bonomy, on the 31st of August, 2006, that it would have been the grossest miscarriage of justice if the Prosecution's written witness evidence had been presented without cross-examination and confrontation, you shuddered to think what might have happened without cross-examination. I submit that the case being presented by the Prosecution now in writing and orally is primarily the same pre-trial, pre-cross-examination version and therefore must be subject to the same caution and reason for scrutiny that was called for during the trial. Flashy PowerPoint presentations have been presented to provide materials out of context and dress up bare allegations or misrepresentations. The Chamber will recall how this case began, with the Prosecution trying to resubmit wholesale questionable documentary evidence from the Milosevic trial, including footage of strife in South America which they cast as being Kosovo refugees in Albania and then they presented footage of graves predating the indictment as purported evidence under the indictment. Indeed, I submit this is a story of the case thus far has been an overzealous Prosecution seeking victory for its case at all costs even if truth, justice, the integrity of the proceedings and the innocent accused are sacrificed in the process. I have the utmost faith and the experience of distinguished members of this panel will not succumb to the Prosecution's arguments and will not allow these things, including the trial's integrity, to be sacrificed merely to reward the Prosecution. Now, I propose that I begin with something that I was stunned and shocked to hear about in the Prosecution's submissions. My colleague Mr. Stamp asserted that the Podujevo killings by SAJ reservists was the lead illustration, indeed one of only two illustrations that he had to show Lukic had command responsibility over and was directly linked to perpetrators of crimes. Since we have an indictment in this case, albeit a rather general and overexpansive accusatory document, the only crimes Mr. Stamp can be talking about are required to be those in the indictment. Podujevo is not in the indictment, never was charged in the indictment. Why after two years of intense litigation and even more years of preparation on their part is the leading cause for the Prosecution against Sreten Lukic the killings in Podujevo something for which legal liability cannot attach in these proceedings. It does not make sense but it shows how misguided and misrepresenting the Prosecution's submissions are. Remarkably the Prosecution quotes Goran Stoparic, an insider police witness but they cite only to his witness statement which they drafted and they ignore the greater bulk of his testimony, his own words. Why doesn't the Prosecution want the whole story to be shown to the world that is watching these proceedings? Why is the Prosecution afraid of drawing to the Court's attention Stoparic's sworn testimony of how the Podujevo tragedy actually occurred and its aftermath? Simply put, the truth hurts them. They cannot obtain a conviction if forced to deal only with the sworn testimony and the truth. But we must point out and address the testimony, the truth to reveal the Prosecution's deck of cards. Now, Stoparic, rather than being ordered to commit any crimes against civilians, explains how the SAJ reservists at Podujevo had been unloaded from their transport and were waiting for instructions when certain individuals just on their own opened fire. Stoparic verified that during his entire stay in Kosovo as a reservist in SAJ, police superiors never issued orders to kill civilians. That's at transcript page 727. Stoparic further stated that the actions of police officials at Podujevo possibly prevented further killings. Transcript page 725. Most telling is Stoparic's own words at transcript page 744, line 25 through 745, line 7. "Q. Therefore, we may conclude that the killings of those people was not intentional or planned by the SAJ or the police for that matter? "A. I have been testifying several times concerning that event and I kept repeating that no one had ordered anything of that nature. I never ordered such a thing and no one did. I'm quite positive about that." Your Honours, Stoparic could not be more explicit in debunking the myth of the Prosecution's case. These words are the death now to Mr. Stamp's submissions of the key crime he alleges against Lukic, the non-indicted Podujevo that he perhaps is prosecuting in some other case but surely cannot be seriously prosecuting here. We have a wide range of evidence that the Serbian MUP in Podujevo not only reacted quickly to the crime by saving survivors, offering medical assistance, and doing an on-site investigation, but also gathered up all the SAJ reservists and sent -- not just the shooters, and sent them on their way back through Kosovo. Paragraphs 316 through 323 of our brief details some of the evidence in these efforts. I will not repeat that, but I do feel I have to highlight a portion of the testimony of Mr. Stoparic at transcript page 748 through 750. He described how the commander of the SAJ was swearing at them and took them out -- took out the SAJ reservists and was angry at them. He said: "I still remember clearly his words and I can quote them quite precisely if you want me to. "Q. I don't believe that is necessary but you may as well if you want the Trial Chamber to hear it. "A. His behaviour was such that one could conclude he was very worried about the things that took place and in his brief speech he told us: You are not the people to be counted on, one can't work with you. I was under the impression that he wasn't very happy about the things that took place. "Q. Were you under the impression that this incident was a shock for the other policemen as well? "A. There was a person, a man whose nickname was Vuk, Wolf, he was a very good professional, an SAJ officer and he used even harsher words. He even took one of the children out to the street to bring him to the ambulance that was there. None of the members of the SAJ as far as I could see was happy about that, were not happy but they were probably horrified." How can anyone using common logic and reason draw from this testimony the inference that the Podujevo killings were intended, ordered or planned by the MUP? Only Mr. Stamp, I submit. Stoparic himself testified that on the bus ride back from Kosovo the SAJ reservists were criticised and chastised and the perpetrators were eventually arrested and eventually convicted and more importantly, the perpetrator was not redeployed to Kosovo again. All the other testimony and evidence from this Prosecution through Stoparic, through Vasiljevic is that there's no other crimes alleged against the SAJ reservists, or some like to call them and try to engage in guilt by association, former Skorpions, during their entire stay in Kosovo. Now, the entire lack of authority by Lukic over the SAJ and their commander Trajkovic is discussed in our brief at paragraphs 410 through 415 so I'll not go into details about this. But as for Mr. Stamp's focus on the fact that the judgement against the perpetrator of the shootings came too late in 2003, this conveniently avoids the evidence led from several witnesses about the functioning of the MUP and the judiciaries in Serbia. And the fact that the work of the police and duties and responsibilities of the same cease upon the presentation of the criminal denunciation report and file to the prosecutor with the prosecutor being independent of the police and bearing all further responsibility to prosecute the case. This was testified to by Judge Danica Marinkovic, transcript pages 23469, 23471, 23472, and also by witness Dragan Furdulovic at transcript page 24744 and 24749. Another matter that the Prosecution fails to bring to the Court's attention is the testimony we had that Sreten Lukic after becoming chief of the public security sector and assistant minister after the democratic government was elected into power, in that position he authorised measures to permit the surviving victims of Podujevo to be safely and securely brought to testify against the perpetrators resulting in a conviction of the maximum sentence. We had testimony from Mr. Furdulovic about that at transcript page 24708. I am shocked that Mr. Stamp believes that someone who exercises his official duties to assist in the protection of witnesses and bringing them to court to reveal the truth and obtain justice is to be considered a criminal. Now if I can move on to another point a closely related matter. There were two charts that were -- well, there were multiple charts but there were two charts I want to focus on from the brief and from the closing arguments. Annex E is the chart on the structure of the MUP forces in Kosovo during the indictment period. There is no citation to the record to indicate where this information was proven and upon which the OTP relies; however, we know this to be the exact same chart produced long before the evidence opened and without hearing the evidence by the then-OTP in-house expert Captain Philip Coo, formerly of the Canadian navy -- Canadian army, who since that time has been disqualified, and rightly so, for not being a proper expert witness and who never was presented as an expert on the MUP. It is simply astounding that the OTP would try to recycle such assertions in this case, which had not been credibly adjudicated or supported by the trial evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think -- well, just a moment, now that -- perhaps you want to reflect on what you've just said. That may be its impact, but I hope you're not suggesting that is its deliberate impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, no, the impact of presenting such evidence leads to that regrettable possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Also, Your Honours, we have annex C and the Prosecution has also identified at paragraph 7 of their submission which is supposed to be a death chart. I actually looked through this, Your Honours, and calling it a proof of death chart is not only misleading, it's inaccurate. If one includes such a chart, one at least ought to highlight the fact that hidden deep within is a concession by the Prosecution that there is no proof from this trial from any of the victims listed in the indictment that they actually are deceased and no proof of bodies or proof of the manner of death. Likewise, the proof of death chart demonstrates that the Prosecution is trying to assert criminal liability for unscheduled victims, an incredible 15 for Krusa that are not in the indictment, and that is the case for some of the other crime scenes as well.

utterances.text: Is that a convenient time to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I should make it clear to you that we are very conscious of the difficulty that's posed by trying to establish the death and the cause of death of large numbers of personnel, that there may be aspects of the chart you're referring to which fail to provide all the detail that one would wish.
