utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour, for that and I will try as hard as I can. I know we're all anxious to try and get these proceedings concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I think Lord Bonomy wants you to be relaxed and speak nicely is what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I could just finish up on the annex relating to the death charts and focusing on the words of Judge Bonomy before the break about these charts being important for showing persons who were murdered. I would point out and perhaps Your Honours have already seen, so but the charts also have persons for which the forensic evidence shows they died non-violent deaths, that is to say they were not murdered. You have Agim Hyseni from Vucitrn, who died a natural cause of death. Some had respiratory problems, Hyseni Kada. Some had unascertained causes of death. So I would ask you to look at that evidence very carefully to see what it actually does prove and why the Prosecution is providing it. As to Vucitrn, the witnesses that the Prosecution called did not testify to the massacre of civilians that the Prosecution keeps presenting. They testified as to one or two persons, a handful of things, and we have the exhibit of Sabrit Kadriu, P2377, where this witness is not giving names based on any kind of personal knowledge that could be considered proper evidence in this trial. He's merely reciting a list that he and others compiled based on information gathered after the fact with no regard to the nature and manner of the death nor even the location. And perhaps that explains why we have persons listed for Vucitrn who were not killed but had, as I indicated, natural causes -- natural and non-violent causes of death. So I ask you to look at that carefully. Moving along. Ms. Kravetz on behalf of the Prosecution talked rather briefly about the Milosh Giliq Street in Djakovica incident and curiously she claimed that there were no KLA in Djakovica in April. This quite simply is incorrect. We have the benefit of the cables that were sent to and from the American State Department which rely upon their sources, intelligence and others on the ground, information which was received by this Defence and which is allowed to be unclassified for use in these proceedings under Rule 70. These sources cannot be argued to be unauthentic. They cannot be said to be prepared or influenced by the accused and they are contemporaneous with the events alleged. If we look at just a few of these I would highlight 6D1637, 6D1638, and 6D1639, they are covered at paragraph 155 of our brief. We see that the KLA not only was in Djakovica, it controlled a quarter of the city itself and was actively trying to take over the city centre. It controlled all the area around Djakovica, again all according to the information available to the US State Department. Under such circumstances where the Djakovica SUP doesn't even control its own city, let alone the entire area under its jurisdiction. How can they have been sure of everything that was going on in the city interior? We have the testimony of Mr. Zlatkovic who showed the chaos that was prevailing in Djakovica resulting from the NATO bombings, the daily attacks of the KLA, and fires resulting, power outages, et cetera. He confirmed that the SUP Djakovica knew nothing of the tragic events at Milosh Giliq and therefore nothing could be done about it or reported. How was Sreten Lukic who was dodging NATO bombs in far-away Pristina with no phone lines to Djakovica, how was he supposed to know about this event? Indeed, the daily situation reports or bulletins that my colleague Mr. Lukic talked about prepared by the MUP staff based upon the reports that were sent by courier from the SUPs was the method of communications available. These reports show, as indeed the Prosecution concedes at paragraph 1091 of its brief, these bulletins do not include Milosh Giliq nor the Suva Reka killings, for that matter, even though they include reports of other crimes that were being investigated and processed. Now, the problem with the Prosecution is that they think that this is evidence that the crimes were being hidden by Mr. Lukic and the MUP staff. We submit otherwise, that they show that they were not aware of these incidents and therefore could not have been put on notice of these crimes. We have dealt with Milosh Giliq -- with the Milosh Giliq incident in our brief so I will not go into more detail on it, but I will highlight the fact that the evidence before this Panel is that this tragic event occurred at the hands of persons from the neighbourhood with evidence of these persons engaging in drinking and perhaps drug use. There's no evidence that the persons were acting in their official capacity, in any official capacity with the police whatsoever and only one is said to have been a firefighter within the SUP. Simply put, the facts do not support the overreaching allegations of the Prosecution. Now I wish to turn to Suva Reka. Ms. Kravetz for her part briefly dealt with Suva Reka and the Berisha killings. Again she indicated and represented to you that there was no KLA presence and no fighting going on. I have to point out that this is yet again incorrect, albeit not critical to the events in question because we have the testimony of one of the participants, but we do have evidence that one-half of Suva Reka was in the hands of the KLA. That's at transcript page 25443. Now, as I said, this is not material to the Court's consideration of this incident because of the following. But first of all let me correct another part. Mr. Stamp talking about Suva Reka claims that Goran Stoparic gave evidence that Colonel Mitrovic and his unit led the so-called Operation Suva Reka wherein the Berisha family members were killed. Now, Goran Stoparic did not, in fact, testify at all about Suva Reka and likewise there is no evidence that the Berisha family killing took place as part of any operation. The perpetrators alleged were all members of the OUP, that is to say the ordinary town police department but neither Ms. Kravetz nor Mr. Stamp seemed to be interested in the specific facts or details of this crime and tragedy, but Your Honours must be, for that is what you have to base your decision on to do justice. The best witness we have for this incident is the Prosecution's own K-83, another touted police insider. This is a man who was a participant in the event and an eye-witness participant in the actual murders themselves. At no point in time did this witness ever allude to or indicate that he and others received any instructions or orders to shoot at or kill anyone, least of all the Berisha family members who were in the pizzeria on that day. In describing how the event transpired and how and why his cohorts began shooting and threw grenades into the pizzeria, the witness illuminated how misguided and wrong the Prosecution's theory is, for after on their own and without warning shooting several persons outside the Berisha home, the individuals involved consumed an astounding two bottles of one litre each of hard liquor. And how did they drink it? The witness said like water. That's at transcript page 3990. Then in the stupor of their private drinking party they proposed to one another on their own accord again that they throw grenades into the pizzeria, which they did and which they followed with shooting. There's no operation, no plans or orders from the police superiors. Look at transcript page 3988 and 3989. This crime is tragic, but as it boils down to it, it is a private act and conduct of persons perhaps drunk or perhaps on their way to getting drunk engaged in a frolic, a departure from any official duties that they could have had with the OUP Suva Reka. Now, the Prosecution cites to efforts by the perpetrators and others to cover up this crime by removing the bodies or some of the bodies. There simply is no credible evidence that Sreten Lukic had any role in the burying of bodies at the firing range or their subsequent removal. It is clear that the event was hidden at the level of the perpetrators and locals of Suva Reka. We have evidence that when the Prizren SUP sent a criminal investigative team to investigate the initial bodies of males who had been killed outside the Berisha home, they were not told about the pizzeria incident nor taken there, and in fact one of the perpetrators of the crimes served to provide security for the investigative team and of course he didn't mention anything about what had transpired. We have evidence that, as was established in Belgrade where this case is subject to criminal investigative proceedings, not even the OUP chief in Suva Reka had knowledge, this is from 6D1631, paragraph 64. With no one reporting the incident, there cannot be any notice and any subsequent duty to investigate or discipline, and the evidence is clear that neither the OUP chief, the SUP chief, nor the criminalistic police in Prizren had any information on this event, and therefore the information reported to the MUP staff did not contain any information about this event. So accordingly as to this indictment -- as to this incident there cannot be established any breach of duty or act or omission leading to the liability of Mr. Lukic. I would stress that this is the very same Sreten Lukic who to the contrary was instrumental until the efforts to illuminate this crime, to have it investigated and then turned over to the prosecutorial authorities when he was the assistant minister and head of the RJB. Indeed we heard from Witness Furdulovic and other evidence including 6D1068 and transcript page 24699 through 24701 as to the proper discharge of his duties by Lukic authorising the interviews of witnesses and suspects who were employees of the ministry per the requirements and the rules as his position holds and the support that he gave to the investigations that have ultimately resulted in this case being pursued in Belgrade against the actual perpetrators. Lukic never refused or held back authorisation for anyone to be interviewed as part of the investigation, showing his openness and professionalism, not a man with anything to hide. We will return to that later. Moving along to Kotlina, which Ms. Kravetz highlighted in the oral submissions last week. Curiously this is one of the few times in their closing arguments that the Prosecution did not have the assertion that there was no KLA presence in the village. Perhaps because we have the paragraphs of the KLA headquarters found in the village, the pictures of the deceased persons with weapons near their bodies, near the bunker that was in the shape of a well, too much evidence for the Prosecution to overlook. However, they do claim that "extensive" evidence supports their case when in fact it boils down to one witness, Mr. Hazbi Loku for whom the forensic evidence, even that of the Prosecution contradicts vital aspects of his claim. Now, the Prosecution did not touch much on the forensics in their oral submissions. At least they did not dwell on the actual forensic findings. They merely wanted to misstate that the forensic findings corroborated the manner of death described, but the forensics do not, in fact, corroborate the Prosecution theory of how this event occurred. I would point to the substantial discussion of this event and the findings of the forensic pathologist and expert Dr. Stankovic. His experience in the field is very significant and I believe that at the end of the day looking at the submissions and the evidence you'll find that missing body parts and impossible placement of bodies and injuries tell a tale different from that presented by the Prosecution. And surely given this forensic evidence, it is not possible to say that the only or even the most reasonable inference of what happened is the OTP side, particularly not when their star witness describes injuries and a manner of death for named persons whom he supposedly eye-witnessed that do not coincide with the forensic evidence of the Prosecution. Surely this shoddy evidence would be an affront to the integrity of these proceedings if accepted. I think we have discussed Izbica in our brief and have adequately addressed the evidence that was led by the Prosecution and illustrating the forensic problems with the Prosecution's case and that evidence; however, as the Prosecutors have raised that in their closing arguments, including Mr. Cepic, I have just a few points to highlight. Liri Loshi and his vaunted tape. The forensic evidence and the forensic examination of -- forensic testimony of Dr. Stankovic saying the bodies are not filmed in their natural positions at the location of death or what's called the situs. Forensics, this time of the Prosecution in their written evidence, say some of the graves never had any human remains in them. Prosecution witnesses say that the bodies -- that bodies were even brought from elsewhere and buried there months later, albeit the witnesses for the Prosecution give conflicting numbers as to the total number of people that perished and/or were buried at Izbica. The neutral evidence in this case shows a strong KLA presence in and around Izbica and continued combat in the area over a span of months with civilians present every time. So no one forced them to leave, and, Your Honours, a critical fact that the Prosecution either did not know or did not bring to the Court's attention and Liri Loshi had to have known and did not bring to the Court's attention but which was revealed by KLA documents and the testimony of General Bislim Zyrapi, Chief of Staff of the KLA, Liri Loshi was the KLA commandant for Padalista, this is far from independent, trustworthy evidence. All this together provides the highly reasonable and we submit almost certain inference that the Izbica evidence was fiddled with, was staged by the KLA. Addressing Mr. Cepic's remarks that the military prosecutor transferred the case to the civilian prosecutors, when was that? Where are the documents? Was it when the military courts were shut down after the war because then all pending files were transferred. Your Honours, this is no more than smoke -- more smoke than substance from Mr. Cepic. We direct you to review the evidence that is before you, not Mr. Cepic's allusions to evidence that is not before anyone. We think the evidence is clear that the Prosecution has not proven the case as to Izbica that can be the basis for a conviction against anyone in this courtroom. Your Honours, I will briefly move to what was said about sexual assaults briefly, for two reasons. First, because I cannot say much without going into private session and I think that we have covered that in the relevant portions of our brief, our final brief, but briefly also for another matter, because despite the prominence of the allegations of sexual assault in the opening statements, which we've highlighted in our portion of the brief dealing with this, and the provenance of allegations of sexual assaults in the closing arguments, it must be remembered how very little evidence was actually led by the Prosecution in this case and presented about sexual assaults. This is not a case about persons alleged to be direct participants in a sexual assault or rape, and thus it must really be shown more than the mere fact that such and assault occurred. People, the right people had to know about it and it had to be part of a widespread and systematic plan for purposes of these proceedings. Respectfully, Your Honours, the purported sexual assaults of a handful of persons by unidentifiable persons -- by unidentifiable perpetrators does not make a case before this Tribunal against these accused, and again I have to keep pointing out how remarkable it is how the Prosecution chose to present its case. They knowingly presented K-63, the husband of a victim, and used his testimony to allege conclusions about the perpetrators, the colours of uniforms, their association with the police, et cetera. They then did not ask the actual victim to identify the perpetrators. I asked the victim about -- when I asked the victim about this, she not only told us about her husband's problems differentiating colours and other concentration problems that would affect his credibility as a witness, of which the Prosecution surely knew of if they interviewed the persons. She also flatly refuted his identification of the perpetrators, saying that they certainly were not the Serbian police. Now, the Prosecution ought to have had this information. They did their investigation. Why would they present such inaccurate evidence on such a critical matter? And let's not forget that K-63 was also the witness who repeatedly denied speaking with the Prosecution in advance and in preparation for his testimony and only relented after the Prosecution itself admitted to such contact. Are we to believe that K-63 is really credible evidence? I suspect not. And again I will not belabour the point because we have covered sexual assaults in our brief. Now, another thing that astounded my from the oral presentations of the Prosecution was that they seriously suggested that due to the fact that the border region saw heavy bombing, it was illogical for persons, Albanian civilians or anyone for that matter, to willingly flee in that direction. Now, as a corollary to this it was presented that identity cards were taken as a planned widespread and systematic method of identity cleansing - I think that's the first time we heard this word - identity cleansing at the border to try and erase all records of the persons' existence and in this regard it was also seriously suggested by the Prosecution that using Pristina as an example they would show the same tactics were used throughout Kosovo, that Pristina was an exemplar and model for all. First and foremost, it is entirely logical and supported by the evidence that a land invasion by NATO was feared by everyone, that the air war was hitting all within Yugoslavia, albeit the hardest in Kosovo. Therefore, we submit, it is entirely within the bounds of human logic that persons caught in a war zone would want to try and escape from that war zone, and to do that you have to go where the bombs aren't falling. NATO was not bombing the countries surrounding Yugoslavia, and for Kosovo residents the closest choices were Macedonia and Albania and therefore it was highly reasonable and logical for persons to cross dangerous ground to get to an area of safety. I simply cannot believe that the Prosecution would try to say that that is illogical or impossible. Such a stance is incredible. Also we have evidence that the roads and bridges near the border with -- with -- near the Kosovo border with these countries were not bombed by NATO, perhaps with an aim towards a ground invasion and perhaps in view of the fact that the refugee flow was resulting from the bombings. Either way, this deeply undercuts the representations made by the Prosecution. We have evidence from Mr. Zlatkovic and from other sources of the situation where multiple convoys of Albanian civilians heading back to their villages from the border were bombed by NATO, Meja, Bistrazin near Djakovica. We even saw the footage, the video footage of the efforts of the police including Mr. Zlatkovic to assist victims of the NATO crime. So I submit it does not support the Prosecution's assertion. Now, as to this newly coined identity cleansing, we have the considerable testimony that even assuming for the sake of argument, arguendo, that identity documents were taken, this act would not in any way erase the records of one's existence nor prevent one from entering back into the country is seeking replacement documents. In this regard we have the testimony of Mr. Vucurevic and of Mr. Dujkovic that there was simply no way to filter out and destroy only Albanian citizenship records because the original books were kept in duplicate and they did not differentiate based on ethnicity. Likewise, there was significant evidence that no such orders existed for the taking of identity documents. Mr. Ognjenovic from the Vrbica border crossing testified that the Albanians were doing it on their own. Even after passing the border in the no-man's land between Yugoslavia and the other side. He and his men collected the documents, preserving them, sending them to issuing SUPs in accord with the law and then eventually left a sack at the border crossing upon their withdrawal, turning that over to the international officials that monitored the withdrawal. Nobody was destroying these documents. Efforts were being undertaken to preserve the documents. But the most compelling evidence on this score ought to be considered from Ms. Kravetz who said that the pattern for this crime came from Pristina which served as a model for the rest of Kosovo and Metohija. There is a slight problem with this picture, however. Not a single one of the witnesses that this Prosecution brought from Pristina testified that their identity documents were taken from them at the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing. Indeed, we had Ms. Bala, Mr. Kabashi, K-63, K-62, none of them testified that they had their personal documents taken or destroyed while passing through Djeneral Jankovic. What does that mean? Likewise we have three witnesses from Urosevac of the Prosecution, Mr. Hyseni, Mr. Krasniqi, and Mr. Bucaliu, all of whom also went through Djeneral Jankovic and who again did not testify that their documents were taken away or destroyed, because they weren't. We had two other witnesses, Mr. Shaqiri and Mr. Qamil from Gnjilane who went through the Globocica border crossing and they too did not have their documents taken away. Not a single one of these witnesses brought by this Prosecution supports their case. And yet Pristina, and I presume the border crossing the Pristina witnesses went through is supposed to be the linchpin to their identity cleansing experiment. I submit that if Pristina is a model, that with the other evidence indicates that there was no plan to take identity documents. And of course let's not forget that there was evidence persons crossed into -- from Kosovo into Montenegro and Serbia proper also without having their documents taken away from them. So what are we left with on the part of the Prosecution? Let us not forget one of their star witnesses as to this identity cleansing, Ms. Sadije. For the moment let us not focus on a fact that she changed her testimony 180 degrees from her sworn statement nor the conflicting accounts of how she was being shot, when she was shot, et cetera. The Prosecution cannot change her testimony and cannot change the fact that this testimony was shown to be false by the official response from the government that she did not previously have issued identity documents and also it's remarkable given this plan that she was successful to get proof of her citizenship, this plan that the Prosecution alleges of erasing person's identities, that one of the persons was able to go in the year 2008 and get proof of citizenship issued and get identity documents for the first time at that time. So this story of identity cleansing and destroying all trace of persons who left, it's not true at all. This case it shows you can't come up with a big fancy buzz word to try and cover up just how weak your evidence is in this matter, and surely the Trial Chamber, as experienced it is, will not fall for such a ploy on the part of the Prosecution. Now, the Prosecution's case is dependent upon the assumption that persons did not leave Kosovo and Metohija for reasons other than criminal reasons, that is to say the criminal plans or actions of Yugoslav and Serbian forces. This is the basis of the expert report by Mr. Patrick Ball and until recently this was the mantra of the Prosecution. But in the closing statements it is not any longer said that the crimes themselves made them leave but simply that the "actions" of forces was "mainly" the reasons persons left. This is at transcript page 26778, lines 3 through 7, and I believe it was Ms. Kravetz. This is intriguing and baffling, but it is a concession on the part of the Prosecution, a telling one I think, conceding that their prior allegations and arguments, including those of Mr. Ball, are not accurate. Certainly there are a whole bunch of actions of armed forces that are legitimate in nature and which cannot be the basis for criminal liability of these accused that are the legitimate and understandable reasons -- that there are also legitimate and understandable reasons for people to become frightened and/or leave their homes and the country, particularly in the middle of a war zone that are not related to crimes. Some examples from the evidence have been cited in our brief, and by way of example the Chamber will recall the testimony of the SUP chief from Gnjilane, Mr. Gavranic. First of all, recall that this man persuaded a convoy of Albanian citizens -- Albanian civilians to return to their homes, arrested persons engaged in crimes against Albanians, and in the end was requested by one of the witnesses -- the Albanian witnesses here to provide a -- to provide an escort for their convoy, which he did, to escort them wherever they wanted to go. In short not even the Prosecution can attack the credibility or good character of this witness. Mr. Gavranic testified as to his knowledge of persons leaving, and this was precisely because of the NATO air-strikes, that it struck military installations in the nearby area near these settlements in Gnjilane and when troops legitimately redeployed to other areas, the citizenry wanted to leave for fear that the nearness of these forces to Gnjilane and the villages in Gnjilane would draw NATO strikes and thus present the possibility of collateral damage upon them if NATO missed or used excessive force. Now, Gavranic explained how he and his officers tried to persuade people to stay but they were adamant about going. This is at transcript page 22700 through 701. Well, given how small we have heard Kosovo and Metohija is, imagine the situation that during daily air-strikes, both the Yugoslav Army and the Serbian MUP are constantly having to move around to avoid being hit, changing their locations even multiple times in a day, et cetera. Well, this activity of troops of the VJ and the MUP is not hostile, is not combat, is not even malintentioned, but it still can bring the civilian population to fear risk from NATO bombs, not from the forces themselves. Now, to get a full grasp of the picture, it should be recalled what amount of forces that we're talking about that would be legitimately moving around to avoid being struck by these NATO bombs that were seeking them out wherever they were. We have evidence that the MUP strength was 10.021, approximately, before the war and grew to 15.000 during the war period. On the VJ side we have 6D-164, page 2. As of the 18th of April, 1999, 71.668 members of the Pristina Corps. Imagine what these units of the VJ and the MUP spread out over Kosovo and moving around, it is legitimately reasonable to assume some civilians left because they had fears that NATO was going to strike these forces and perhaps strike their villages. However, this in no means is conduct that can be labelled criminal on the part of the Army of Yugoslavia or the Serbian MUP. And if this is the type of conduct the Prosecution is relying upon when it says actions of forces rather than crimes led people to mainly leave, then the indictment in this regard must fail. While we're talking about reasons why persons left I would be remiss if I did not note that Patrick Ball not only engages in creating his own science, as my colleagues pointed out and as the expert testimony of Dr. Fruits provided. The exercise of Mr. Ball also engages in extraordinary creation of a new psychological study, because although the Prosecution fails to provide us with any of the credentials of Mr. Ball or criteria used by Mr. Ball or credible sources of Mr. Ball in the field of psychology, it does expect us to embrace and accept as true Mr. Ball's conclusion that fear among civilians from bombings lasts only two days and then dissipates, which of course would conveniently allow him to remove fear of bombing as a potential reason for flight and thus re-affirm his own results. Congratulations, Mr. Ball. But I submit that is not a proper way of conducting evidence at a trial. Now, again the Prosecution selected Pristina and highlighted Pristina as the role model, the suitable model for how things happened elsewhere in Kosovo during the indictment period. Well, let's look at Pristina and what the evidence has to offer for us. I think the most instructive place to look is the evidence provided to us, thankfully, by the Rule 70 provider, the United States of America who produced 6D1637 which has information based upon their own contacts on the ground in Pristina during the height of the war. This exhibit provides that both ethnic Serbs and ethnic Albanians in Pristina were becoming increasing concerned, huddling together in bomb shelters, and growing afraid and uncertain because NATO started bombing during the day. It further says that due to the bombings, there is a lack of work, many factories are shut down, and many persons, including ethnic Serbs, are leaving the city, because with lack of work they are not being paid and do not know how to make ends meet in Pristina anymore. This is very substantial evidence. This is something that does not fit into the Prosecutor's neat little picture nor in Mr. Ball's theorys, but it is a fact, uncontroverted evidence in this case, evidence that I think warrants a close scrutiny of the Prosecution's allegations. The reserve police detachments, RPO. I honestly had thought I would not have to discuss the RPO too much, but with the insinuations that the Prosecution and Mr. Cepic made in closing arguments I see the record has to be set straight. Both the Prosecution brief and I think the submissions of Mr. Cepic mix and match reserve policemen with the RPO, as if they are the same thing; they are not. As a preliminary matter it is our position, and I believe it's born true by the evidence, that the RPO were disbanded with the start of mobilisation and the proclamation of war as military conscripts and reservists had to go to their wartime units and reserve policemen therein had to go to their police posts. This is borne true by discussions held at meetings at the premises of the MUP staff. I think P1996 is one example. Now, the genesis of the RPO begins with Exhibit P1415. We see that document does not mention the MUP staff or the MUP for that matter having responsibility for this. From P2166 we see that it is not Lukic or anyone from the MUP talking about the RPO, and indeed the RPO and the defence of villages was something that was part of the global plan to suppress terrorism, and Mr. Djakovic told us who drafted that plan and that no MUP members were involved. P1114, from this document dealing with the area Kosovska Mitrovica we see that the RPO in the town of Vucitrn is entirely made up of 32 VJ reservists, not a single reserve policeman, and the RPO in Cvjenarej [phoen] is commanded by a VJ reservist, commanded by a VJ reservist, has one police reservist and 110 VJ reservists. The documentation is clear that the RPO comprised primarily of army reservists and therefore when mobilisation and the war were called up these bodies ceased to exist because mobilisation would be impossible and it would be impossible to grow to the record -- to the number of 70.000 members without the RPO disbanding. It should be recalled that even Mr. Cepic presented evidence that army personnel could not be commanded by the police, apart from being labelled police and having communicated with the police and having some police reservists therein, the RPO did not have a role within the Ministry of the Interior command structure. The MUP have lists of them because in accordance with the law they had to keep lists of everyone who had legally possessed fire-arms. P1063, P1060, P1065 all are communications within the Ministry of Defence. None are sent to the MUP. I hope that answers the questions posed by Mr. Cepic. And further I would only note that Mr. Cepic has provided no proof for his assertion at paragraph 757 and in his submissions yesterday -- or yesterday that the RPO continued to exist after the mobilisation declaration of war, none whatsoever. The minutes from the SUP staff meeting state otherwise. Paragraph 754 of the Lazarevic submission says that many had military uniforms due to lack of police uniforms, but surely that's not true because VJ reservists are given VJ uniforms. 755 of the brief of Lazarevic states that Mitic claims that there was a problem with unauthorised registration of men who were military conscripts by the MUP and there is a document cited, 5D1014 and also I think you need to look at P1415 because you'll see that the registration was actually done by the military district in Pristina, not by the MUP. And again, 5D1014, this document is dealing with reserve police, not the RPO. Again, the military defences keep misconstruing and misunderstanding how the police works. But in the end we would submit that the Prosecution has presented no evidence of the involvement of any of these persons in any crimes. Turning back to P2166, Mr. Hannis the other day commented that one of his favourite exhibits was P2166. I don't know if it's because they cite to it so much in their brief, because they do, but I submit that they ought to have spent more time reading it because they surely don't. First off, I think we would be remiss if we did not take into account the testimony of a witness brought here by the Trial Chamber, General Dimitrijevic, himself at the head of the intelligence security service of the VJ General Staff for many years and who testified that no stenographic notes or minutes were kept at these type of meetings and that P2166 does not correspond to his recollections of the same. This is at transcript page 26597 through 26599. Likewise, Dimitrijevic also concluded that P2166 was written at some later date and does not accurately reflect what was said. That's at transcript page 26615. Respectfully, Your Honours, Mr. Hannis's favorite document has to be considered in light of Mr. Dimitrijevic's telling testimony. Going further, it is important to take a look at what is actually contained in the document and what precisely is attributed to Mr. Lukic and what the author of this document, Susic, has put into it, recalling that there's been some indication that this was put together from several meetings. Lukic in his briefing as set forth in the document nowhere is attributed as actually uttering the words "Joint Command," and further, the briefing by Lukic focuses exclusively on what would be considered routine police affairs. Others talk of the conduct of actions under the general plan for suppression of terrorism as we have indicated. And now as for the references to the Joint Command in this document, it must be taken into account that General Dimitrijevic testified that the name Joint Command was in fact not used during these meetings and in fact did not exist. In reality, what does Mr. Hannis's favourite exhibit really tend to show us anyway, that the highest state leadership of Yugoslavia and Serbia was convening meetings. Isn't that the job of such organs in every country. Is the state of the union speech in the United States some big criminal conspiracy just because the legislative members, executive members, and governmental organs are present? Is it a crime for a servant of a state to meet with the president of the country to report on activities of the governmental organ? Well, I have yet to see any support for either of the foregoing being a crime or proof of a crime, and I would submit if it were, jails around the world would be full and countries governmentless. The propositions being made by the Prosecution simply are not, are not the only, let alone the only, reasonable conclusions or inferences to be drawn from the evidence, no matter how much Mr. Hannis likes this exhibit. Another topic we need to briefly touch upon is the evidence of trains and the evidence of Mr. Bucaliu. It is truly remarkable that the Prosecution would steadfastly cling to the flawed testimony and analysis of Mr. Bucaliu that has already been discredited at trial, but at transcript page 26781 through 26782 Ms. Kravetz in claiming the frequency of number of trains was increased again cites to Mr. Bucaliu. The problem with this logic and argument is the same as it was during this trial. Common logic and mathematics coupled with the Prosecution's own exhibits, the very same exhibit brought by Bucaliu debunked his claims soundly. Looking at P1331, that is the train log-book from Bucaliu we see that 228 trains were registered for the 78 days of the NATO bombing campaign. Bucaliu himself testified that the regular traffic was about ten trains a day. Now, that would amount to 780 trains during the stated time-period of the NATO war and the indictment period. Bucaliu testified that P1331 was authentic and that all trains passing through had to be registered. So if the regular train traffic was ten trains a day, there should be something more than 780 trains that were registered in this book. There were not. Indeed, there was no increase in trains but rather a drastic decrease. Now, it should be noted that this contradiction was itself acknowledged by Judge Bonomy at transcript page 3044 that the OTP is continuing to promote such damaged goods as this evidence is quite telling as to the weakness of their case. We have set forth in our brief the evidence establishing that all joint anti-terrorist actions were conducted in 1998 pursuant to the global five-stage plan with all actions being planned and maps being made by the Pristina Corps and that 1999 the functioning of the joint actions was conducted in the same manner. And again, we had -- as my colleague indicated, we had the person most involved in the VJ and MUP interactions, Milan Djakovic, come and tell that he and the corps drafted the plan, made all the maps, et cetera. Now, I do have to touch on some issues of VJ and MUP interactions since I need to satisfy Prosecutors Hannis, Stamp, Kravetz, and Cepic and to clarify some points. It boils down to not understanding how the police operates and not analysing the documents. Indeed, the Law on Defence is important to understand the activities of the police during war and so are the instructions received from the ministry leadership in Belgrade. 6D269 dated February the 18th, 1999, is an important document for you to consider, it comes from the chief of the public security sector General Djordjevic and demonstrates the genesis of VJ and MUP interaction and indeed the communications between the two. Section 16 of Djordjevic's dispatch is also important. It directs all MUP organs to get in touch with other state organs, such as the -- and including the VJ. This dispatch is not limited to Kosovo, rather, it tasks SUPs all throughout Serbia, all throughout Serbia, to get together with the VJ in the area in regard to exchanging information with the aspect -- or with the defence of the country in mind, a perfectly legitimate and reasonable and logical instruction. This was also sent to the MUP staff in Pristina and this is the reason why Lukic had meetings with the military generals. Those are the meetings he's talking about in his interview which the Prosecution has latched on to. These are perfectly legitimate meetings and these are not any kind of parallel institution bypassing the MUP or otherwise -- the MUP chain of command or otherwise establishing some sort of separate command. Let me touch on the Lukic interview. Your Honours, respectfully, the translation is horrid and the questioning by the OTP is horrid. They mix terms and topics and do not accurately reflect what was discussed. We have previously filed an objection on this topic and stand by it. Take note that the Prosecution provides the term Joint Command to Lukic. Lukic starts off saying in his interview so-called and then adopts the Prosecution's shorthand because they keep repeating it so much. But they, including the interpreter, don't even always use the same term, the same Serbian term to describe it. Sometimes it's "zdruzena komanda" and sometimes it's "zajdnicka komanda." But Lukic is clear these are merely meetings to exchange information and we submit they are in compliance with the instructions from chief of sector in 6D269. Now it should be noted that this dispatch and those that follow it from Djordjevic and which are in the record never once tasked anyone in Kosovo, anyone from the MUP in Kosovo with getting in touch with a Joint Command. If such a thing had even existed in 1999 wouldn't Djordjevic, chief of the RJB, and someone who the Djakovic notes show was present for a large number of these meetings that have somehow come to be labelled Joint Command wouldn't he direct people to go to it? And doesn't it follow if he's directing people to go to meetings with the army at the level of each SUP, is the Prosecution's case -- does it mean that there had to be seven or eight more Joint Commands somewhere in Kosovo? It just doesn't make sense. Another matter for the Prosecutors including -- and also Mr. Cepic to consider which I think Your Honours will see right away. The dispatches from the MUP in Belgrade sending the PJP units to Kosovo, look at the language there, 6D291, for instance, the PJP detachments are not sent to Kosovo to be deployed at the MUP staff or to take orders from it; rather, the language used says that they are sent to the assistance of the SUPs, they go directly to the SUPs. If the PJP were to be under the MUP staff, then it would be logical for them to be deployed to the staff but they are not. Very telling and yet very much ignored by the Prosecution.
