utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What the Prosecution also ignores is the evidence that they themselves have presented. I apologise, I didn't have it on the right channel to hear the interpreter's request. I will slow down. What the Prosecution also ignores is the evidence that they themselves have presented. I do not have time to highlight all the errors in the Prosecution's brief. Later I will highlight some egregious ones that relate to my client; however, for the moment I would like to focus on some that relate just to Lukic's interview. Paragraph 228 of the Prosecution brief in claiming that the Joint Command issued orders for joint actions and that Lukic acknowledged this and that his role was to ensure that the orders were carried out by the MUP, well, first of all, there is simply no citation in the brief for this assertion that -- as to what Lukic's role was. That part is sheer fabrication by the Prosecution. As for the Joint Command commanding the actions, the Prosecution cites to the Lukic interview, and I think it is instructive to read this part so I would refer Your Honours to take the time to read page 49 of the Lukic interview and to see that it does not in fact mention any Joint Command task in commanding these actions, rather, Lukic says very clearly, very succinctly that the tasks were defined by the Pristina Corps for joint VJ and MUP actions after the general decision by the state leadership to adopt the global plan in 1998. That is exactly what the other evidence in this case has proven. His interview is consistent with it. The only thing that is not consistent is the reading and inference that the Prosecution provides for this, which is not even remotely possible, given the plain language of the interview, and for this they seek life in prison given a mis-characterization of the evidence. That is something that I am shocked and disgusted at, Your Honours. Another matter that needs review, the allusions in the brief at paragraph 219 of the Prosecution that Lukic admitted that his predecessor had command over certain special units. Your Honours, I would tell you to closely check the pages cited from the Lukic interview because my reading of the same reveals that Lukic is talking about the time he became chief of the RJB, that is to say 2001, not when he became manager of the MUP staff in Pristina in 1998 and 1999. Lastly on this topic the Lukic interview was cited several times in the brief, for instance, at paragraph 1004 of the Prosecution and by Mr. Stamp in his oral closing remarks to demonstrate that Lukic admitted to a dual reporting by the PJP to him as well as to the PJP commander Lieutenant-General Obrad Stevanovic. Your Honours, it's truly and honestly a shame that the Prosecution did not read the interview, perhaps because it was a poor translation, perhaps because there was no transcript until February of this year, even though the interview was taken sometime in I believe 2003. Lukic in this section that they cite is talking about the year 1998 and 1998 alone. During that time-period the commander of the PJP, Obrad Stevanovic, was in Belgrade most of the time and Lukic and the staff in Pristina had obligations toward the Kosovo Verification Mission to report manoeuvres, police presence, et cetera, to pass along communications. You'll recall that Mijatovic, his deputy, was the main liaison of the MUP with the mission. Likewise, the staff acted as a logistics forwarding communications to Belgrade and from Belgrade, a post office, if you will. That is the sense in which the dual responsibility is talked about. But in 1999 logic and common sense dictate that when the commander of all PJP, assistant minister, head of the police administration, Lieutenant-General Obrad Stevanovic comes down to Kosovo, as we've heard in the evidence, when he spends the entire time, the entire Kosovo war at the MUP staff, using the staff as his own office as his mailing address, as we heard from several witnesses, there is no need for any dual responsibility. Stevanovic is there. He remains -- he remains as the commander of the PJP, he remains to be the last person, the last member of the MUP to withdraw from Kosovo and Metohija. So the role of the staff in this regard ceases, particularly with the KVM no longer on the scene. You really have to look at the context of the evidence, Your Honours, not stitch together a patchwork of assumptions and misquotations as the Prosecution has done. Ljubinko Cvetic, he was highlighted in the Prosecution's oral submissions and as well as in the written submissions. This vaunted police insider witness whom Chester Stamp rallied to the defence of in his oral submissions, well, the final brief of the Prosecution is replete with citations to incredible propositions for many of which the sole evidence of record is Ljubinko Cvetic. Now, however, Mr. Stamp does not seem aware that Mr. Cvetic's evidence is inconsistent with the proffered command chart of the MUP, the document prepared by Philip Coo that we -- we have the Prosecution presenting again. And, Your Honours, we had our discussion before, I am told that that chart is, in fact, tendered into evidence as P255.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp does not seem aware that Mr. Cvetic's evidence is inconsistent with this chart. Is it a case of seeking out victory rather than truth and justice? I don't know. But we have a very interesting thing. The linchpin of the Prosecution case against Mr. Lukic is Exhibit P1505. Ljubinko Cvetic is the key insider witness against the police, the former SUP chief in Kosovska Mitrovica. What did Ljubinko Cvetic say about P1505 in these proceedings? Nothing. The Prosecution failed to present it to him. Why would they fail to present such a key bit of evidence to one of their key witnesses to comment on? Could it be that they were concerned that he would not give them answers that were supportive of their case? Not a single Prosecution witness, fact or expert, was presented as to the nature and scope of P1505 in the functioning of the staff. Multiple witnesses were presented by the Defence demonstrating that P1505 did not come to life as my colleague Mr. Lukic pointed out. The Prosecution here has a live witness that they failed to present this to. They are relying upon a mere document to prove their case. Remarkable. Incredible. Now, in short, since I know we're -- I'm trying to condense as much as I can, the topics for which Cvetic is used within the Prosecution's brief are the so-called Joint Command and the MUP staff. However, we must take into account that Cvetic, according to his own testimony, never was a member of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija, that's at page 8146 of the transcript. Now, this flies in the face of a critical averment to the Prosecution, again which is based on P1505, and they claim that all SUP chiefs were part of this expanded MUP staff managed by Sreten Lukic. How is it that the OTP's key police insider witness negates this claim soundly? Ergo, the Prosecution's claims as to P1505 cannot be supported by their own evidence. Secondly, as Mr. Cvetic was not a member of the MUP staff, Cvetic cannot be considered to have reliable, credible knowledge about the activities of that staff. Now, in a similar nature Cvetic testified under oath and very explicitly that he was never present nor participated in any information exchanges that the VJ General Djakovic has christened as the Joint Command. His testimony in this regard is at transcript page 8080, lines 16 through 17. Now, coincidentally while we're on the topic Djakovic testified a few times that he had a habit of interpreting things via or utilizing military shorthand or terminology or logic. It is interesting to note that in discussing coming up with the informal name for these meetings with Mr. Pavkovic that Djakovic used the term command, both in describing the MUP staff, he calls it the MUP command, and for the meetings themselves. It should be noted in this regard that when questioned about the regular offices of the MUP staff he conceded that by his military logic any office is to be considered a command post. That's transcript page 26456 and also 26521. Thus, Djakovic's use of the term command must be taken with a grain of salt, as otherwise it can lead to mistakes in interpretation given such a dilute and lax criteria for something being referred to as a command according to him. Now, returning to Cvetic, by ordinary logic his allegations relative to these meetings cannot have a high level of probative value or credibility. He simply doesn't have first-hand knowledge. Now, this is especially true given the evidence we have of Cvetic and his behaviour whilst acting as the SUP chief in Kosovska Mitrovica. The Chamber ought to be reminded this man defended by the Prosecution was actually dismissed from his post in the middle of the war because his SUP had not undertaken to uncover and investigate a single crime on the territory, see P1989 in this regard. He boldly claimed that not a single policeman was processed for the murder of an Albanian in all of Kosovo and Metohija. While this was perhaps true for his SUP while he ran it, it certainly is not true nor corroborated by the evidence of record. Indeed, after he was removed, even the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP returned to its job of investigating and processing reports of crimes and detaining or arresting perpetrators and submitting them for prosecution, including MUP employees. See, for instance, the testimony of Mr. Bogunovic in this regard or the exhibit relating to JSO reservist Goran Vasilinovic [phoen]. We have had multiple witnesses testify as to the charges investigated, processed, and filed against perpetrators of crimes including police members, civilians, and VJ members. We have some of that in the portions of 6D614 that were admitted into evidence. There simply is no way for the credibility of Cvetic to stand in the face of such overwhelming documentary and testimonial evidence to the contrary, particularly when it is alleged that he hid in the basement of the SUP and neglected his official duties to investigate crimes. Paragraph 276, and there's others in the Prosecution brief relying upon Cvetic, therefore must be disregarded to the extent they claim a lack of investigations and the evidence is contrary to this fact. We have heard the evidence presented by various witnesses as to the investigations conducted by the MUP, the creation of the KiM dossier to collect and continue investigations as to crimes committed, the testimony of 62, Mr. Kostic, Mr. Furdulovic, and even K-84, among others, in this regard and we have the KiM dossier with the 20-odd thousand files that one of the witnesses testified to, several dozen against police members for murder all processed properly, cases against civilians, cases against the VJ. Simply put, there's no way to account for the wide disparity between the evidence and Mr. Cvetic's testimony of no processed cases at all, at least not in any way that preserves the testimony of Cvetic. General Drewienkiewicz or DZ, I must make a few comments to draw to the Chamber's attention another of the Prosecution's vaunted witnesses. First of all, the Prosecution cannot, as we have said time and again, make up for their own failure to call a police expert by asking military and lay persons with no training or knowledge of the Serbian MUP to opine on what they believe the role of Sreten Lukic was and what the staff did. For one thing recall that all of General Drewienkiewicz's interactions would have been through a translator and we have seen how difficult it can be for certain things to translate correctly. Documents in this case by the KVM and by military personnel have given a variety of titles for Sreten Lukic, almost all of them incorrect. Proper evidence must be analysed as to Sreten Lukic's role and authority as we presented it already. But returning to General Drewienkiewicz, please recall, Your Honours, that General Drewienkiewicz was sent as deputy head of the OSCE-KVM mission to monitor and verify, among other things, one of the main things that he was supposed to do down there was the withdrawal of the agreed number of MUP forces from the province. Now, we've heard testimony and evidence that the KDOM stood in place of the KVM, negotiating agreements on behalf of the KVM, one such agreement was this base-line agreement that we've heard about, the 10.021 policemen that were allowed to remain in Kosovo and Metohija. We saw a Rule 70 document confirming the withdrawal of the specified number of police and we saw the documents about this reduction. Shaun Byrnes, the head of the US KDOM who negotiated the agreements, told us about this base-line, told us that all documentation was turned over to the KVM and that he personally told them and gave it to them. General Maisonneuve, the KVM sector chief in Prizren, a subordinate of General Drewienkiewicz, he knew about the base-line and compliance with the reduction. However, for some reason General DZ spends from October to March of the next year in Kosovo and Metohija supposedly to verify the police draw-back of forces and claims that the Serbs refused to give him a base-line figure and that he does not have a base-line figure. KDOM was uncooperative, KVM never had a base-line. What on earth was Drewienkiewicz doing on the ground in Kosovo? How is it possible everyone around him including his own subordinate had access to and knew the base-line and he didn't? This is simply too incredible to believe and we must question the real reason for Drewienkiewicz's presence and deployment to Kosovo and Metohija as a result. It should be recalled that General Drewienkiewicz refuted another subordinate's claim, Ciaglinski, that he handed over evidence of burned passports to him for safe-guarding. Drewienkiewicz did not verify that. How could he not remember that if it happened? It didn't. Ciaglinski's claim in that regard can also -- Ciaglinski's claims included the horseshoe plan which Drewienkiewicz also refuted, as did -- as did Colonel Kotur and other evidence that we have, including from Prosecution witnesses such as Pesic, Loncar, and Abrahams, who debunked the existence of said plan, and indications are that the horseshoe plan was a myth, a hoax thought up by German intelligence to bolster support for the war. This Trial Chamber must take such information with a grain of salt and certainly, certainly the evidence of Drewienkiewicz does not come up to par to convict someone for 20 years to life. Just briefly on two witnesses utilised by the parties in their oral submissions, Shaun Byrnes and K-25. First of all, K-25 did not have any personal dealings with the staff and he was not in a position, we submit, due to his rank and function to make any valid conclusions about the functioning of the staff or even the planning and command of actions, how that was undertaken. He was at too low of a level. Shaun Byrnes, this is a man who testified after August 1998 the VJ did not participate in any anti-terrorist actions, and yet we have a whole bunch of other evidence that in fact all operations were the legitimate anti-terrorist actions of the VJ and the MUP. His credibility is put in doubt by the fact that he could be so wrong about this point. Now, likewise, for all his complaints voiced here about Lukic and MUP, remarkably the Rule 70 documents from the United States authored by him and by others contemporaneously about the events do not have the same information nor the same complaints. This is very curious indeed. Why would you say one thing publicly to the press and to the world and then say something privately when reporting to your superiors? You have to take into account the very significant evidence of his contacts with the KLA, his encouragement that they save quality troops to be used later, a reverence to what Joksic testified about meant the spring offensive that the KLA was planning. You have all those rather detailed information sheets from the RDB, I think there was seven of them, of suspicious contacts between Byrnes and KLA members. And then you have Byrnes who does not even try to explain any of that. He just blanket denies them all like they didn't happen. This was not my translator, no, I was never there. The last time I heard such a blanket denial without explanation, respectfully -- the last time that I heard such a blanket denial without explanation, respectfully, was President Clinton with respect to Monica Lewinsky and he was ultimately found to have -- the blanket denial turned out not to be accurate. I suspect that is the case here as well. But what is more revealing is the Rambouillet negotiations and we heard testimony that Shaun Byrnes himself arranged for and permitted the KLA leadership, persons even he called criminal terrorists to carry guns onto the plane and take them to the peace negotiations in France. Have you ever heard of such a thing? Imagine what kind of information and mistruths did Byrnes have to give and what he had to hide to get -- to get that past the officials at both airports that criminals were carrying guns. That goes towards his credibility, which I submit is quite suspect and marred. Vasiljevic, Aleksandar Vasiljevic, I would be remiss if I did not take a few moments to review this star insider witness of the Prosecution of the VJ's military intelligence branch. Now, albeit the testimony of Vasiljevic did change quite a bit from his sworn statement, including the testimony in the Milosevic trial as regards the MUP and the way he testified here. Originally in his statement and in Milosevic Vasiljevic tried to place blame for an event in Gnjilane to the SAJ that he calls Skorpions. However, at trial in our proceedings he did admit that it was a VJ group that was responsible for the same and that his service had no evidence of any post-Podujevo crimes by the SAJ reservists whom he calls Skorpions. And as my colleague indicated, Vasiljevic admitted that Lukic was the ninth piglet or the lowest ranked at the meetings, at the one meeting he attended but this was only after being confronted with the transcript and the video recording of his own words. This is the witness we're supposed to believe. Until he gets caught with his pants down, he'll continue to say a lie. His credibility is suspect and it ought to also be recalled that he was a suspect before he became a favourite of the Prosecution. So you have to recall even he said, well, I gave that interview as a suspect, I may not have been telling the truth. In any event, given his propensity to say untrue things and then later correct them, one wonders if it's a matter of time before he corrects everything false that he has said. One such falsehood that he did not get around to correcting was his testimony that among the JSO were persons who had a combined 150 years of jail sentences, according to information from his service he says at the time. Unfortunately for him and the Prosecution, General Dimitrijevic, the Trial Chamber's own witness and himself the former head of the VJ military intelligence refuted Vasiljevic, saying that VJ intelligence had no such information. This is at transcript page 26755 through 26756. So of course we can't take Vasiljevic's claim for this and there is no other evidence to show that this is -- that this would be true. It should be noted in this regard that at the time of formation of the JSO Vasiljevic was actually retired, whereas Dimitrijevic headed the intelligence service. So who are we going to believe has the more -- better intelligence or information, Vasiljevic or Dimitrijevic? Another factor the Chamber should take into account is the sworn testimony of two of the subordinates of Vasiljevic, indeed the very persons that he pegged as the source for his allegations about various crimes by the MUP in Kosovo and Metohija. That would be General Stojanovic and Sergej Perovic. Both testified in the defense of the co-accused, General Lazarevic, and asserted that investigations by their service could not confirm any of the alleged crimes and indeed Perovic denied ever having reported to Vasiljevic anything about bodies at a bus station in Kosovska Mitrovica, thus the value of Vasiljevic's testimony is decreased, I submit very significantly. And lastly on this topic it ought to be pointed out in the bodies there at Djakovica, I apologise, not Kosovska Mitrovica. So the value of Vasiljevic's testimony is decreased particularly since Perovic was situated in Djakovica. Now, Vasiljevic does have a reason to shade his testimony against Mr. Lukic. Let's recall that he was arrested by the MUP, by the RDB and imprisoned for some time, as he testified to. He had some run-ins with the RDB after that during the time of the Kosovo conflict and similarly he has another reason to shade his testimony against Mr. Lukic for when Lukic was head of the RJB in 2003 and during the anti-corruption crack-down led by the police under Mr. Lukic after the assassination of Prime Minister Djindjic and called the sabri or Sabre Operation, Vasiljevic's colleague and then the chief of VJ intelligence General Tomic was indeed apprehended and detained as part of this corruption crack-down. Now, the Prosecution's final trial brief presents unsupported assertions that present an incomplete, incorrect, skewed and unreliable record of the proceedings that have been conducted to date. As I think I said, I cannot point to all the of them, for we do not have time for that but I think I have a duty to assist the Trial Chamber by handling some of the most egregious and representative of these absurdities. As to the -- Your Honours, I'm told by my colleagues that it's time for a break. I thought we had another 15 minutes in this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we would have a break in about five minutes or so, I imagine, but I thought you might be winding up anyway and that we would allow you to complete our submission and then have our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I can do that probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, very well, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As to the MUP staff, the Chamber will find in the Prosecution's brief an assertion by the Prosecution that the RDB chief in Kosovo, David Gajic, was a member of the staff and that the JSO commander Legija was also a member. I ask you to note that the citation given for these assertions which gives the impression that the citations are supportive of these assertions is 180 degrees s counter. They cite to Joksic, a Defense witness who spent a great deal of time negating this assertion and proving that Gajic and Legija were not members of the staff. If one reads the citation to the record provided by the Prosecution, all that the references say is that Gajic was head of the RDB in Kosovo and that Legija was head of the JSO. None of the cites offered support the OTP proposition which is the linchpin of their case. This is incredible misrepresentation of their brief. You will also see in the brief, I don't have the citation in front of me, but relative to Gornje Obrinje. It's one of the only citations to Gornje Obrinje. You will see that witness Paunovic and other witnesses testified that the killings in Gornje Obrinje were retaliation by the VJ and MUP forces. Not a single one of the citations says this and not a single witness was called or led to make such a preposterous claim. You cannot believe a word of what is contained in the OTP's brief because they make a mockery of candour and honesty in their citations. Looking at paragraph 197 closely, neither -- the Gornje Obrinje paragraph is paragraph 62 of the OTP's brief. I thank my colleague for that assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm not prepared to sit back any longer and listen to allegations of lack of candour when there have been many instances in this trial when the Lukic briefs have been less than accurate without the allegation being made against you of lack of candour. Do you consider that what you're doing is an appropriate way to be addressing us in regard to matters which do not simply on the face of your assertion justify that claim?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, perhaps candour is a strong word but I submit when these allegations and when this document is being presented and asking for 20 years to life in prison, depriving someone of their liberty for the rest of their life, that's a very serious matter, and when after two years of trial the citations are exactly 180 degrees the allegations, and I'm not talking about one or two but all throughout, that is a very serious matter especially when it's the Prosecution doing it. And so therefore, I only ask that the Trial Chamber take very careful notice of what is being presented by the Prosecution and what actually they are citing to because in my opinion, they as the Prosecution have a duty to present a truthful account of the evidence. And if the evidence says one thing and they -- and indicative of innocence and they twist that to make it indicative of guilt, it's certainly something that is a cause for concern in my book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we'll break now because I'm going to listen to what you've said. I don't think it's been recorded in the transcript, and then we'll deal with it after the break and that will be at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivetic, your actual remarks were that the Prosecution submissions make a mockery of candour and honesty, and that's just one of a series of remarks that bear the interpretation that there is a deliberate attempt on the part of the Prosecution to mislead the Bench. Now, we recognise the highly charged atmosphere which surrounds this stage in the proceedings; nevertheless, we regret that you have not had the courtesy to recognise that the language you've just used is not appropriate language for counsel appearing in any Tribunal. At this late stage in the proceedings, we choose to simply record that we do not accept that there is a basis for claiming that the Prosecution deliberately set out to mislead the Bench. Now, please continue and complete your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, and for the record I think you'll note that I did upon recollection say that I just wanted the Chamber to take close note of the citations and make sure that they support what the Prosecution alleges in the part just before the last break, and really that is all that is important here is to make sure that truth and justice are done. With respect to religious objects, I will just state that we have had evidence of SUP chief from Prizren, Vojinovic, that of the over 15 mosques in his city, not a single one was damaged during the war. That's at 6D1532, paragraph 29, as well as transcript page 24198. And now the final part of my submissions about Sreten Lukic the person. I will not belabour the submission to point to the specifics of his health condition. Through our confidential filings relative to provisional release earlier in the case they are of record. The Chamber has access to his health there and we urgent you to take them into account and also to seek a report from UNDU for an update as to his health now. Sreten Lukic according to the evidence was instrumental in investigating and urging an investigation by the Serbian authorities of war crimes not only in Kosovo but elsewhere in the former Yugoslavia, a man who exerted so many efforts to promote and foster the rule of law and to establish meaningful cooperation with among others the ICTY. You heard the testimony of Kostic, Furdulovic, former Prime Minister Zivkovic and even the Prosecution's own insider witness K-84 crediting Sreten Lukic as the man responsible for directing the MUP to illuminate and investigate and prosecute crimes, even those within their own midst. Prosecutions are now underway in Serbia including sometimes against police personnel for individual crimes committed in Kosovo, including Suva Reka, for instance, as one of the indictment locations all because of the courage that Sreten Lukic had and his good ethics and professionalism in empowering the police to investigate everyone and anyone, including those in the MUP. You heard about the efforts under the tutelage of Lukic to establish the KiM dossier and you heard that the MUP established full cooperation with the ICTY even before the Government of Serbia had established a law and a formal obligation to do so. Lukic, like any good policeman in Serbia, sacrificed to uphold the law and order and for the greater good. It was not very popular to take the stand that he did when he became chief of the RJB, to reform the MUP, to arrest persons, and stamp out corruption in Operation sabre, including persons with connections to political parties in the government. I recall -- I recall and I ask you to remember evidence presented by a protected witness in this case that death threats were issued against Lukic by Serbs for his stance against crime and in investigating the crimes of the past during that stage. The democratic changes in Serbia were congratulated and supported by the West including the ICTY and in that atmosphere Sreten Lukic was selected as the best possible person to lead and reform the MUP. And I think if you convict such a person you have to think about what kind of message that would send to the outside world about those who would take the hard road and stand up for law and foster investigation and prosecution of crimes, and indeed I submit that a conviction in this case would stifle any future persons in a similar situation. Indeed, a conviction would reward the Prosecution but it would also encourage future generations to hide crimes rather than fight against and investigate them, because what is the use of being a professional, committing your life to illuminating, investigating, and preventing crimes if at the end of the day you can be held just as accountable as the perpetrators merely by -- because of guilt by association or the fact that you wear the same police uniform as some of the persons. This would be the first time that a subordinate like Lukic is charged for what is alleged and purported to have been said and done by his superior officers, such as Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic, deceased; deputy minister and chief of the RJB, Lieutenant-General Djordjevic; assistant minister and chief of the police administration and commander of the PJP, Lieutenant-General Obrad Stevanovic; assistant minister and chief of the UKP, General Dragan Ilic. Lukic cannot stand in place of these persons. Just because one is deceased and the OTP is choosing him to be the poster child for their case does not change the fact that the Prosecution has made a mistake. For Lukic is not a perpetrator of crimes. If anything, the evidence shows he is a victim. We would ask you to acquit Mr. Lukic on all counts and in every respect as to the Prosecution's indictment, and at this time I would like to say it has been an honour and privilege for myself and for Mr. Branko Lukic to represent and act as counsel for Mr. Sreten Lukic, who we feel is a very just person. At this time I have two corrections for the transcript. I will state them. If the Chamber feels that they need to be verified they can be done so. At page 73, line 6, I was talking about General Tomic, T-o-m-i-c, the transcript reflects a different surname. And at page 71, line 22, it is reference should be to the JSO, whereas the initials in the brief I think state JAS or something of that sort. I hope that that can be located and corrected. That is I believe all for the Lukic Defence, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. However, Mr. Lukic indicated a desire to say something to rectify the omission of references to paragraph 72(C) I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I can get ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] We are dealing with deportation from Srbica, paragraph 72(C), the village of Vocnjak, Kladernica, Turicevac, Izbica, Tusilje, and Cirez. At the beginning of the NATO bombing they were in the area of deployment of the KLA which was confirmed and expounded by an OTP witness, Mr. Zyrapi. There were KLA headquarters in some places such as Turicevac where the headquarters were in the school and people kept joining up there. We have that in P2241, the statement by Hadije Fazliu. Witness Hadije Fazliu says on the 26th of March Serb forces shelled the village of Turicevac but there were no casualties they went to the village of Tusilje, which means going in-depth into KLA territory. Now this method of movement and capturing civilians was something Mr. Zyrapi testified to, IC105. He drew the withdrawal of the KLA into regions F and then G. So the KLA is using the civilians as a human shield. Witness Fadija Fazliu in a statement also says that on the 29th of March in the village of Tusilje police and military forces arrived and he says that of the policemen that they were dark blue camouflage uniforms. OTP witnesses such as K-25 and K-79 and then Defence witnesses Vladimir Ilic and Zivaljevic, Nikcevic Radojica, and others testified that the police units which took part in the anti-terrorist actions, the PJP, in 1999 wore green camouflage uniforms with combat vests where it was clearly written in front and at the back the word "police." From the village of Tusilje and Turicevac where in the area of operations at that time when an anti-terrorist action was being carried out in the area of Drenica and that is order number 455/73, otherwise P1968. The witness says that they were told to go to Klina, which meant pulling out the civilians from the combat zone. The witness also mentions that in passing through her own village of Turicevac she stayed on in the village and that no forces arrived there but that they had no food. Once again, P2241. When the witness Hadije Fazliu says in her statement that on the 1st of April policemen arrived with civilian vehicles and that they were wearing uniforms and that they asked the citizens to go to Glina [as interpreted], the witness does not describe the uniforms and she refers to these men as policemen who arrived in civilian vehicles, civilian cars. Therefore, there's no certain indicator of the fact that they were policemen of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia at all. After they reached Jasenica they returned to Brocna the following day. She says that at the border crossing they weren't asked to show any ID cards or produce any money. In the entire statement the witness doesn't say at any time that anybody ordered her or other civilians that they had to go to Albania. If we look at the dates of the movements, and this is -- if you compare this to the statements of Milazim Thaqi from which it emerges that at the same time in the direction of Djakovica from Izbica his family was moving along that route and that the Serbs returned them to the village of Tusica -- or rather, Kladernica and Izbica. That is P2246, the statement by Milazim Thaqi, page 6, paragraph 5. And that the witness wasn't stopped anywhere by the police or escorted by the police or followed by the police anywhere, which meant that she could go back because nobody forced her to go to Albania. The witness Rrahmani Xhevahire, an OTP witness, says in her statement that two days after the bombing from her village of Bukos with her extended family she went to the village of Kozica. That means at her own initiative she left her own village. This is shown in Exhibit P2239, page 2, para 6. From this we can see that the reason, exclusive reason for these people leaving the village was the start of the NATO bombing. Three days later from Kozica they set out for Srbica. However, the police returned them to the check-point, at the check-point sent them back, and they decided to go to Glodjane to her husband's uncle where they stayed for some ten days. So they decided where they were going to go themselves. After that, they decided to go back to Kozica. Defence witness Bogunovic Nenad testified in the following manner. He said in the region of Cirez and Kozica on the 29th of March, 1999, there was not a single police unit present. The Exhibit is 6D614, paragraph 97. Witness Rrahmani in his statement says that in mid-April while they were in Kozica which is high up in the mountains they saw a unit in Cirez three or four trucks and several tanks and in the regions of Kozica and Cirez in mid-April there were no MUP units. This can be seen from an order of the 37th Motorised Brigade in point 5 of that order, 11, which defines independently without the MUP reconnaissance work being carried out. It is P2239. I apologise. Apart from P2239 you can also see it in 5D1029. Also in the combat report of the 37th Motorised Brigade dated the 19th of April in point 4 the state in the territory it is noted that NATO on the 18th of April in the evening hours acted against the brigade units in the village of Cirez, that is to say targeted the units in Cirez, and it is 5D1023. Also in a report of the 37th Motorised Brigade of the 21st of April, 1999, point 2, it is stated that the 3rd Motorised Brigade was deployed in the region of the village of Cirez. 5D1087 is the relevant exhibit. And that in the region of Kozica and the village of Cirez at the beginning of April there were no MUP units present, and this is confirmed by an order of the 37th Motorised Brigade of the 4th of April, 1999. It is Exhibit P2813, point 4.13.(redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] We have to redact this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That will be done. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution witness K-24 in a statement dated November 1999 with respect to the events in Cirez at one place says that she is -- that a policeman came to the door of the cellar wearing a dark blue camouflage uniform. That is P25848. However, during the cross-examination of this witness she showed her clothing. She was wearing black and she said that the policeman was wearing that same colour. The transcript is 4792, lines 7 to 22. In her statement she mentioned no hats. She didn't mention that anybody was wearing hats. She describes in her statement of 2006, however, seven years later she says they were wearing hats and she said that they had a double-headed eagle emblem and the emblem of a tiger. There is no evidence to show that anybody of the Serbian members had a tiger or a double-headed eagle as their emblem, members of the MUP, that is. OTP witness Salihu Abdullah in his statement when he explains that he was taken prisoner with a group of men on the 29th of March, 1999, states that some of the members of the Serb forces on their shoulders had blue, yellow, and red bands. That is P2255. As far as members of the MUP are concerned, the bands began to be worn on the 15th of April, as we said today, and there were never three colours worn at the same time and this can be seen from 6D237. The same witness in his statement says that when they were taken to Glogovac into custody they were beaten and that the policeman who secured them allowed a paramilitary to separate one of the men, Rahman Topilla, and that he then killed them. He also said that they were interrogated by Momo Peljevic who ordered another policeman to beat them. Defence witness Petar Damjanac who was the chief of Glogovac officially up until the 1st of May, 1999, and came several days later after that in no way had any knowledge about anything like that ever having happened. Now, as far as the inspector is concerned, Momo Peljevic, witness Damjanac claims that an inspector like that never existed in Glogovac or in the entire Pristina SUP for that matter and that is at transcript page 23769, lines 7 to 15. Witness Salihu who at the end of his statement says that when the war was over and when the Serbs withdrew he returned to his village of Baks and says that his family was still in Vucitrn. Therefore, the family was in Vucitrn throughout. In a statement witness Salihu explains that he was taken prisoner on the 20th of September, 1999, in an action launched by Serb forces that lasted for three days, that is Exhibit P2255, and that he was in the triangle between Baks, Vrboc and Cirez himself. At the time in that area we have the 37th Motorised Brigade present carrying out anti-terrorist actions in which the members of MUP did not take part and this can be seen from a report of the 37th Motorised Brigade, Exhibit 5D1036 and 5D1058. And this is supported by the combat report of the Pristina Corps dated the 2nd of May, 1999, 6D1470, point 1, last paragraph. This witness explains the kind of uniform of the men killing the prisoners, shooting them, and although he was in the immediate vicinity he did not mention any insignia or markings that can be linked to the police. He explains that all the members of the paramilitaries who took him prisoner had Seselj's insignia and blue eagle, a square with a blue eagle, but no police unit had such insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect you did say something after "insignia" and didn't just collapse, so thank you, Mr. Lukic, for your submission. Now, you've already heard that there will be some Prosecution rebuttal. Can I ask of the Defence whether any Defence counsel intends to say anything or at least to seek to say anything in rebuttal of any other Defence submission. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as you may suppose, I don't know what my learned friend Mr. Hannis will say, although a lot was said at the expense of my colleague Mr. Cepic who has been moved to the other side of the courtroom. There are many things that do not deserve any comments. So we will have just 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I'm concerned only at the moment whether you have anything to say in rebuttal of anything submitted by any of the other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour, with respect to the sixth Defence team we will speak for 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. And Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to my colleague Mr. Ackerman, two to three minutes; and I hope so Mr. Hannis and I will not have to disappoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in connection with the Lukic Defence I have two or three references for the transcript to add to what my colleague Mr. Lukic said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we've decided to do is to hear Defence rebuttal at this stage because in the course of rebuttal something might be said that has an impact on the Prosecution case when it's too late for the Prosecution to say anything about it. So we want you to treat discretely what you now have to say about any other Defence case and the first person that has something to say I understand is Mr. Fila. So we'll hear your submissions in relation to your rebuttal of Ackerman now, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I said, I'll be very brief. Mr. Ackerman said that at the meeting in Nis Pavkovic spoke about his request to stop working -- I'm trying to speed up. This is Exhibit P1468, these are minutes from the Joint Command of the 26th of October, 1998. My colleague Mr. Ackerman said that Pavkovic asked that the Joint Command stop with its work, and Pavkovic did put forward a request by the command of the 3rd Army that the Joint Command stop its work because probably by mistake Mr. Ackerman identified Pavkovic with the command in Nis, but at that period of time he was not in the 3rd Army. He was appointed only later on, he was at another post at that time, and a document should be looked at which is referred to by the Prosecutor which is a letter from the federal government from which it is evident that after that discussion these military documents on the so-called work of the Joint Command were sent to Slobodan Milosevic's secretary, that's P1317, and that the Joint Command ceased working. That's the first point. And one should also note that Minic chaired this meeting, which was the meeting before the last, which shows that what the Prosecutor said is incorrect, that Minic presided over the Joint Command until the 14th of September, 1998, but it was rather until the 28th of October, 1998, which means that Minic presided over the Joint Command throughout its duration and this is evident from the fact that he opened and closed meetings and he did that in other situations and you never find that with Sainovic. And the third point that has to be raised is the conclusion of my colleague Mr. Ackerman that the Joint Command should be compared to the combined General Staff of the USA. And all we can say is that the USA staff does not contain any police units so we don't think it's a good comparison, but I do accept that it's normal for there to be coordination between the army and the MUP in wartime. Thank you, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly. Today my colleague Mr. Lukic on page 7 from lines 21 to page 8, line 4 spoke about the testimony of General Milorad Djakovic concerning planning and my colleague Mr. Lukic said that the excerpts of these decisions and maps were delivered to the MUP staff or directly to the PJP units and on the basis of this he said the PJP units and the commanders went into action. I ask the Chamber to look at the testimony of General Milan Djakovic, pages 26396 to 26398, especially transcript page 26398, lines 2 to 13, where General Djakovic responded to Your Honour's questions, to questions of the Presiding Judge, and said some things slightly different. He said that these documents which were received from the Pristina Corps were the basis for the unit commander. And when he received those he had to work for at least four or five hours to draw up his own decision based on that, and then that was the basis for action. So it was the PJP unit commander who issued a command which was the basis for the PJP going into action. Thank you, Your Honours. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it you have nothing to say in rejoinder to Mr. Fila's submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll be very brief and less temperamental, referring to the words of my colleagues Ivetic and Lukic. First of all, I wish to mention the following. I'll start with the decision on the establishment of the MUP staff, exhibit number P1505 in e-court. My colleague Mr. Lukic said that it was never implemented, that we have not, to put it more precisely, found evidence in these proceedings that it was implemented. I would like to refer to the testimony of one of their Defence witnesses and also to the testimony of Philip Coo who on pages 12071 to 12073 and later on 12074 to 12075 explained quite clearly what the situation was which he found in the MUP archives. There were only a few reports not to the number of reports there should have been that the shelves were empty, whereas in the military archives the shelves were full of documents which were all there in good order. One of the Defence witnesses of General Lukic in his statement which is under seal 6D1631 in paragraph 120 explained quite clearly that the PJP reports were sought but were not received and that efforts were made to find them. We saw that they exist because we saw 5D1418, which is a dispatch of one of the police brigades sent to the superior command --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I don't see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Lukic. You were speaking over the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't see that this has anything to do with our closing arguments today. If it's analysis of our final brief, they should have done it before, but this is not rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's rebuttal of your submission about P1505 and that I think -- beyond that, Mr. Cepic has not strayed. He'll be conscious of the restraints upon him at this stage of the proceedings, but what we've heard so far falls within the Rules. So please continue, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Point 2 of that document which speaks of planning, organizing, and control is the basis of my intervention and we have an example 5D1418, a combat report of the 25th of May, 1999. I wish to draw attention to it to avoid wasting time, and I would also like to refer to the allegations put forward by Mr. Ivetic that military judicial organs did not exist or did not operate after the end of the state of war, which does not correspond with the truth. Not only do we have testimony and documents, but it's an indubitable fact that military judicial organs continued doing their job until 2004 or 2005. And clear analysis of all this can be found in 4D171 which is a report of the army prosecutor Stanimir Radosavljevic, where in the paragraph before last investigative activities are mentioned in relation to the site of Izbica which is mentioned here. And let me conclude by saying that Gordana Tomasevic, a Prosecution witness also spoke of this and pointed out that civilian judiciary organs began investigation in that direction. Thank you. I have nothing further to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Ivetic or Mr. Lukic, do you have any rejoinder to any of these submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just this document 5D1418 is self-explanatory, has nothing to do with planning or actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, this is probably a good time to adjourn for this evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would agree, Your Honour, and I would agree to take seven minutes off my presentation tomorrow if we can adjourn seven minutes earlier tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have no need to take seven minutes off your presentation tomorrow. You, as we already indicated, should take the time you feel is appropriate. You've already indicated restraint prevails, but it is not helpful to us to avoid dealing with some -- anything significant on which you feel that we can be further assisted. So anything that's important to the determination of the case, we ought to be fully addressed on within reason. We've changed the schedule for tomorrow since time became available in the morning. We are sorry that we cannot move it earlier, but we're restrained to 10.45. The indications we have had informally are that it may be possible to complete the case within the morning, but we have available time in the afternoon and will not be surprised if at least some of that time has to be used. So we shall now adjourn until 10.45 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of August, 2008, at 10.45 a.m.
